#10500. The midterms weren’t the rebuke of AI money many expected

The midterms are shaping up to be a record-breaking election for Democrats, who have flipped states including South Carolina and Texas. But the election has also shattered records for private political spending. By some estimates, super PAC spending exceeded $2 billion this cycle, more than 50% above previous election cycles.

One of the dominant narratives heading into the midterms was that Big Tech—and the artificial intelligence sector in particular—would spend hundreds of millions of dollars electing AI-friendly lawmakers, much as the cryptocurrency industry had done in previous elections.

Indeed, Leading the Future, the largest pro-AI super PAC network—backed by VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, OpenAI cofounder and president Greg Brockman, and Palantir and 8VC cofounder Joe Lonsdale—invited comparisons to the crypto super PAC network Fairshake, drawing on some of the same donors and political operatives. (Both networks operate through partisan affiliates: Leading the Future has Think Big for Democrats and American Mission for Republicans, while Fairshake has Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs, respectively.)

But as public sentiment toward AI soured and Democratic Party insiders warned candidates against accepting industry money, the narrative began to shift. A Fast Company analysis of election data suggests the midterms were hardly the rebuke of AI money that some had anticipated. More than 86% of the candidates backed by Leading the Future have won or are currently leading their House of Representatives or Senate races. That’s roughly on par with Fairshake, which supported 87 candidates this cycle, 77 of whom have won or are currently ahead.

The two industries’ political efforts also appear to be converging. Leading the Future and Fairshake backed 21 of the same candidates, including Republican Kevin Hern, who won his Senate race in Oklahoma. Hern also received support from the Anthropic-funded Public First, which has positioned itself as a counterweight to the industry’s other political spending operations.

Big Crypto outspent the AI industry but achieved similar results

While Big Crypto outspent the largest AI industry super PACs this election cycle and backed more candidates, the groups saw broadly similar results. Fairshake, the cryptocurrency super PAC funded by Coinbase, Ripple, and Andreessen Horowitz, spent about $154 million this cycle, compared with $34.8 million by Leading the Future and $24.4 million by Public First. Yet roughly comparable shares of the candidates each group supported won their elections.

Of the 12 Senate candidates backed by Leading the Future, nine won their races, compared with five of Fairshake’s eight candidates. Both Senate candidates supported by Public First—Hern in Oklahoma and Republican Pete Ricketts in Nebraska—also won. In the House, Leading the Future’s candidates won 31 of 38 races, compared with six of 11 for Public First and 63 of 79 for Fairshake.

Analysts had previously noted that Leading the Future appeared to be playing it safe, largely backing incumbents. But Fast Company’s analysis found that just over half of its 40 winning candidates were incumbents. The group also spent considerably more, on average, backing non-incumbents: roughly $511,000 per candidate, compared with $288,100 for incumbents.

Several of Leading the Future’s biggest investments paid off. Among its winning candidates were Sen.-elect Julia Letlow (R-LA), whom the group backed with $1.17 million; Rep.-elect Ben McAdams (D-UT), who received $1.12 million in support; and Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY), who received $1.16 million.

But heavy spending was no guarantee of success. Two of the 10 candidates who received the most funding from Leading the Future lost their races.

Arguably the AI industry’s biggest setback came in South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Republican Darline Graham, sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. Leading the Future spent about $2.3 million supporting Graham—more than it spent on any other candidate. Another pro-AI super PAC, Building the Future, poured an additional $2.5 million into the race, the only contest it has reported spending on. Yet Andrews, a former pediatrician, pulled off a historic victory in the Republican stronghold without financial backing from either AI or crypto super PACs.

Leading the Future also spent nearly $1.4 million on Democrat Jesse Jackson Jr., the disgraced former Illinois congressman who resigned amid a federal corruption investigation. He didn’t make it past his primary.

Public First suffered several high-profile defeats of its own. The group spent roughly $13 million backing New York Democrat Alex Bores, who lost his primary. Other losing candidates who received substantial support included Texas Republican Carlos De La Cruz Jr. ($1.5 million), Alabama Republican Rhett Marques ($960,000), and Texas Republican Alexandra Mealer ($905,000).

Fairshake likewise saw some of its biggest bets fail. The group spent $36.8 million supporting Ohio Sen. Jon Husted and another $19.7 million opposing his Democratic challenger, Sherrod Brown. Brown won. Fairshake’s second-largest investment, however, paid off: Alabama Republican Barry Moore won his Senate race after receiving $12.2 million in support.

The group also spent millions trying unsuccessfully to defeat several Democrats, including Illinois Senate candidate Juliana Stratton, whom it spent nearly $10 million opposing. Three House Democrats also prevailed despite Fairshake’s opposition: La Shawn Ford in Illinois ($2.5 million), Oliver Gilbert in Florida ($2.1 million), and Donavan McKinney in Michigan ($269,000).

AI Super PAC spending peaked during the primaries, then cooled heading into the general election

Weekly spending by the largest AI super PACs surged in June, coinciding with the closely watched Democratic primary of Alex Bores in New York. Bores, a New York Assembly member and former Palantir data scientist-turned-AI safety advocate, lost after Leading the Future poured $8 million into opposing his candidacy. The Anthropic-backed Public First, meanwhile, spent roughly $10 million of its $13 million investment on Bores that same month.

Bores lost to fellow Assembly member Micah Lasher, who went on to appear on the general election ballot in New York’s 12th Congressional District. Neither super PAC spent money supporting or opposing Lasher, who was victorious on Tuesday.

But AI money, especially toward the end of the election cycle, was dwarfed by Big Crypto.

In October, Fairshake spent $57.6 million, largely on advertising and media buys, compared with $4.1 million by Leading the Future and just over $1 million by Public First.

Industry observers have attributed that disparity, at least in part, to AI’s growing unpopularity across the political spectrum. A September Pew Research Center poll found that 56% of Democrats were concerned about the impact of AI, compared with 46% of Republicans—a relatively narrow partisan divide in an otherwise polarized political climate.

Even so, both Leading the Future and Public First backed more Republicans than Democrats. Leading the Future supported 34 Republicans and 16 Democrats, spending money to oppose just one candidate: Bores. Of the Republicans it backed, 28 won or are currently leading their races, compared with 15 of the 16 Democrats. Public First supported eight Republicans and five Democrats, while spending $1.4 million opposing three Republicans. Four of its five Democratic candidates won, compared with four of its eight Republicans.

Despite the prevailing view that Democrats see AI money as toxic, Big AI has still spent an outsize amount supporting Democratic candidates. On average, Leading the Future spent nearly twice as much per Democratic candidate than per Republican candidate. 

Public First’s spending followed a somewhat different pattern. Although it spent more overall supporting Democrats, largely because of its $13 million investment in Bores, its median spending per Republican candidate was higher.

That spending came despite a public backlash from within the Democratic Party. More than 100 Democratic operatives signed an open letter urging candidates to reject money from AI companies. Yet the industry’s political spending continued, often with little mention of AI itself. As NBC News reported, ads funded by AI groups rarely highlighted candidates’ positions on the technology.

There is also a convergence between the candidates that Big Crypto and Big AI support. Leading the Future and Fairshake backed 20 of the same candidates this cycle, including New York Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres, whose campaign received $1.4 million from Fairshake and $1.1 million from Leading the Future. Alabama Republican Sen.-elect Barry Moore also benefited from both groups, receiving $12.2 million from Fairshake and roughly $330,000 from Leading the Future.

As public sentiment sours, the industry faces a wave of potential legislative and regulatory challenges. Democratic gains in Congress could mean greater scrutiny of AI companies, which have until now enjoyed powerful allies in the House, Senate, and White House. Proposals ranging from state and federal data center moratoriums to restrictions on the development of artificial superintelligence could help shape the industry’s future.

When the new Congress convenes, roughly one in 13 House members and a quarter of newly elected senators will have benefited from Leading the Future’s support. For a super PAC that didn’t exist two years ago, that’s a remarkable foothold. Whether it translates into political power is another question.

#10499. Jack Dorsey’s Block is cutting jobs again. Here’s what makes these layoffs different

Jack Dorsey’s fintech company, Block, began a second round of layoffs on Wednesday, months after cutting more than 4,000 jobs in February. The company has not said how many employees are affected at this time. 

The cuts hit the Customer Ops, Risk Ops, and Learning & Content Operations teams supporting Cash App, Block’s consumer financial services app, and Square, its tool for sellers. According to Business Insider, those teams will be “reducing the number of roles, changing some responsibilities, and shifting some reporting lines.” 

Affected employees are expected to receive a “separation package and transition support, similar to those affected in February 2026.” Block has not detailed the new terms. In February, laid-off employees received 20 weeks or more of severance pay, with the final amount dependent on tenure. Their packages also included equity vested until the end of May, six months of healthcare coverage, their company-issued work devices, and an extra $5,000.

Block did not respond to Fast Company’s request for comment as of publication. 

The layoffs came one day after Block reported its third-quarter results on Tuesday. The company said it raised its 2026 gross profit forecast to $12.63 billion, up from its initial $12.51 billion estimate. It also projected a fourth-quarter gross profit of $3.32 billion. 

Block hasn’t explained what drove this round of layoffs. Earlier this year, Dorsey announced that the February layoffs were not because of financial issues, but because of “intelligence tools,” like AI.

“A significantly smaller team, using the tools we’re building, can do more and do it better,” Dorsey wrote on X then. “Intelligence tool capabilities are compounding faster every week.”

“We see an opportunity to move faster with smaller, highly talented teams using AI to automate more work,” Block CFO Amrita Ahuja said. 

Block is also continuing to build its own AI products. The company recently released Dessa, a speech-to-speech AI voice model trained on the recording of real human conversations.

#10498. Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU

Over the past years, Meta’s TorchTitan has emerged as the PyTorch ecosystem’s premier clean-room reference platform for large-scale generative AI model training. Built entirely on PyTorch-native scaling primitives, TorchTitan provides an unencumbered, highly modular showcase for pre-training flagship dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures like Llama 3, Qwen 3, and FLUX.

Historically, developers looking to train PyTorch models on Google Cloud TPUs faced some challenges: either undertake a complete codebase rewrite into JAX, or grapple with legacy torch_xla. That paradigm has officially shifted. With the launch of TorchTPU, Cloud TPUs now feature a native backend (torch.device("tpu")) integrated directly into PyTorch's core interface. Enabling a training script to use TPUs now only requires minimal changes to your device initialization code. Providing device compatibility, however, is only half the battle, developers also need high performance production-grade, distributed training recipes. This is where TorchTitan on TPU comes in. TorchTitan TPU is a fork of Meta’s TorchTitan implementation that is adapted to enable model training on Google Cloud TPUs. The fork is available at https://github.com/google-pytorch/torchtitan/

Rather than requiring engineering teams to invent custom TPU sharding strategies or hand-craft low-level XLA communication passes from scratch, Google and Meta co-developed TPU-native execution passes directly inside TorchTitan. TorchTitan serves as the definitive vehicle for scaling PyTorch on Google Cloud TPUs.

TorchTitan provides official, battle-tested recipes for pre-training large dense models (such as Llama 3 70B/405B and Qwen 3 8B/32B), Mixture-of-Experts (such as Qwen 3 235B MoE), and diffusion transformers (such as FLUX.1 12B).

Beyond initial pre-training, TorchTitan serves as the scalable trainer inside post-training pipelines like VeRL for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) alignment. In these workflows, TorchTitan handles the parameter update step while synchronizing weights with high-throughput serving engines like vLLM-TorchTPU.

Parallelism is also kept separate from the model code: techniques such as fully sharded data parallelism and tensor parallelism are layered onto a parallelism-agnostic model implementation. The exception is expert parallelism: the MoE layer performs explicit communication through a pluggable token dispatcher that each backend can implement in its own way.

TorchTitan builds a model from a configuration tree, and that tree can be rewritten before the model is constructed. This offers a clean way to replace individual blocks of a model with versions that run better on TPU, without touching the model definition or the shared trainer loop.

We use this actively. The TPU recipes replace standard attention with Splash Attention, a Pallas kernel that handles causal, sliding-window and packed-document masks without materializing the attention matrix; replace the final projection and cross-entropy loss with a fused Pallas kernel that never writes the full logits tensor to HBM; and replace MoE expert matmuls with grouped Pallas kernels. Each kernel is a JAX function turned into a PyTorch custom op by TorchTPU's torch.tpu.pallas.jax_op decorator, which is all the glue a new kernel needs. Each replacement is a config flag, so a recipe can turn it on, and a test can compare it against the plain PyTorch path it replaces. Kernels can come from tokamax, the OpenXLA kernel library for TPU and GPU.

FSDP2 is built around the GPU execution model. Its all-gathers and reduce-scatters are issued from module hooks as explicit collective calls, and overlap with compute comes from running them on dedicated CUDA streams synchronized with events. None of that is visible to a compiler: the collectives sit outside the traced region, so on TPU a torch.compile region breaks at every FSDP hook and a whole-step graph cannot be captured at all. TorchTPU provides no-op stream and event objects only so that FSDP2 runs; XLA has no use for them, since it schedules work from data dependencies.

SimpleFSDP takes the compiler's view instead. Parameter sharding is a DTensor parametrization: reading a module's weight performs a redistribute from sharded to replicated, which is the all-gather, and its autograd backward is the reduce-scatter. There are no hooks and no explicit collective calls, so both collectives are ordinary nodes in the traced graph, whether that graph is a per-block torch.compile region or the Graph Trainer's single make_fx step. The XLA compiler schedules the all-gathers ahead of the matmuls that need them and overlaps the reduce-scatters with the backward compute, inside one program. Mixed precision is part of the same mechanism, a policy that sets the gather dtype (bf16 parameters) and the reduce dtype (fp32 or bf16 gradients) on that redistribute. Hybrid sharding for multislice is the same code on a 2-D mesh: shard within a slice over ICI, replicate across slices over DCN.

On FLUX this is what brought TorchTitan to 99% performance parity with JAX MaxDiffusion: the per-layer HLO for a SimpleFSDP block is a single module with the weight all-gathers, matmuls, attention and norms fused together, which is the shape of program XLA was built to optimize.

Many PyTorch trainers either run in eager mode with CUDA graphs to cut launch overhead, or apply torch.compile to isolated regions, typically one transformer block at a time. TorchTPU does not yet support the PyTorch torch.Stream abstraction, which limits the performance of mixing eager-based FSDP2 with layer-wise torch.compile. SimpleFSDP helps by expressing parameter sharding in a way that is compatible with compilation, whether using layer-wise torch.compile or full-graph capture.

TorchTitan's Graph Trainer provides full training-step capture (forward, loss and backward), producing one FX graph ahead of time with PyTorch's make_fx tracer, skipping AOTAutograd partitioning, so the whole computation is visible to XLA). GraphTrainer also runs optimization passes: to implement graph-based activation memory policy that decides what to save, recompute or offload. The train step then executes as a single XLA program.

This is the model XLA was built for, and it makes PyTorch training on TPU conceptually the same as JAX, where the whole train step is one jitted function. Owning the whole step as one graph is also what makes the large-model compilation techniques possible: scan over layers, which runs the decoder layers as a single loop body so that compile time and memory stop growing with depth, and the graph splitter, which cuts the step into separately compiled forward and backward programs with activations offloaded to host memory in between. On Qwen3 235B this path reaches 29%+ MFU.

The optimizer can join the graph as well: While the fused_adam optimizer is very performant, a functional AdamW update can be traced into the train-step (functional_adamw_step) and ensures an iteration has no host-side work between the first forward op and the weight write-back. On Qwen3-8B this path reaches 51-52% MFU.

Every lever below is described in the TorchTitan TPU optimization guide, and nearly all of them are already wired into the recipes. For most models, getting a good MFU on TPU is a sequence of configuration changes on an existing recipe rather than new code. The order matters, because each step changes what the next one measures. A lot of optimizations in TorchTitan are available as ready-to-use building blocks that can be enabled by a flag flip (see illustration below).

4. Tune Compiler, Communication and Profile

To check that TorchTitan runs efficiently across different classes of models, we tuned and scaled several of them on TPU v7x (Ironwood). At scale, Llama 3 405B (large dense model) holds about 57% MFU from 128 to 1,024 chips. Qwen3 235B (large MoE model) reaches 32.42% MFU on a single 1,024-chip slice and 30.51% on 8,192 chips across eight slices. Muse Glimmer 30B (modern dense model) reaches 43.4% MFU on 128 chips (4x4x8). FLUX.1 (diffusion model) reaches 19.4% MFU on 1,024 chips (8x8x16).

The following case studies show how we got there for three of these models, each representing a different class:

FLUX.1 is a 12-billion-parameter diffusion transformer, which makes it a useful check that the playbook above is not specific to LLMs. We trained it at 1024x1024 resolution on a TPU v6e-8 with FSDP in bf16 and a batch of three samples. Out of the box, in eager mode with FSDP2 and full activation checkpointing, a step took 11.49 seconds. Applying the playbook in order brought that down one stage at a time. Deferred-and-fused eager execution cut the number of HLO module invocations by 28% and the step to 9.95 s (15.5% improvement). Replacing FSDP2 with SimpleFSDP reduced the step to 6.52 s (52.6% improvement): the trace was dominated by FSDP2 copying parameter shards into a flat staging buffer before each all-gather and back out into per-parameter tensors afterwards; SimpleFSDP all-gathers each parameter directly, so the staging buffer and both copies are gone (see the SimpleFSDP section above). The splash attention kernel, with sequence packing and segment ids so that no MXU cycles go to padding, took the step to 5.55 s (17.5% improvement), and per-block torch.compile, which hands XLA large sub-graphs instead of fine-grained modules and moves control flow out of the Python interpreter, took it to 3.02 s (83.8% improvement).

The final step came from three small, local rewrites in the model code that the profile pointed at: splitting a fused projection into two separate linear layers so its output no longer had to be sliced apart, simplifying the rotary embedding to plain element-wise math, and unpacking Q, K and V with a view instead of a transpose. None of them changes what the model computes; each removes copies and lets XLA fuse more of the graph. Together they brought the step to 2.78 s (8.6% improvement), 4.1x faster than the starting point and about 99% of the throughput of the JAX-based MaxDiffusion on the same hardware.

We also scaled FLUX from 8 to 1,024 v7x chips, keeping three images per TPU. The best configuration went from 2.53 s per step (20.76% MFU) on 8 chips to 2.71 s (19.4% MFU) on 1,024, which is 93% weak-scaling efficiency. Past one 64-chip cube, pure FSDP slows down due to the model’s compact size. Hybrid sharding via HSDP fixes this: it shards within each 4x4x4 cube and replicates across cubes. We used the topology-aware device mesh, which maps the parallelism optimally to the physical 8x8x16 torus.

Muse Glimmer 30B is a modern dense decoder: 52 layers, grouped-query attention with 32 query and 2 key-value heads, a 202k-token vocabulary with a soft-capped output head, and a layer pattern that mixes sliding-window and global attention, with RoPE skipped on every fourth layer. It is the case that shows how much works out of the box. The model definition, the parallelization and the training loop ran on TPU unchanged; the port came down to two model-specific pieces. Upstream implements the sliding-window pattern with FlexAttention, which has no TPU backend, so the first step was a windowed SDPA inner attention that reproduces the window exactly and gives a correctness baseline, checked against upstream on CPU. The second piece was the fused cross-entropy kernel, which we extended to apply the soft-cap to each vocabulary tile as it computes the loss, so the 202k-wide logits never have to be materialized; without that the LM head alone dominated memory. Everything else, including the Graph Trainer wrapper, was the standard onboarding ladder, with each feature behind a flag and its own test. The resulting recipe trains the 30B on 64 v7x chips (a 4x4x4 slice) at sequence length 16,384 with one sequence per device, Graph Trainer plus SimpleFSDP and fp32 gradient reductions, and reaches 5,848 tokens per second per chip at ~44% MFU.

Qwen3-235B-A22B is the largest MOE model in this set: 94 layers, 128 experts with 8 active per token, 235 billion parameters of which 22 billion are active per token. It is the case that exercises the large-model half of the playbook. At this depth compiling the whole unrolled step as one program is not an option: XLA plans every buffer of a program at compile time, and a 94-layer graph laid out flat asks for more HBM than the chip has before a step can run, while its compile time grows with every layer. Getting it to work at all meant enabling one of the two Graph Trainer paths for large models. Scan over layers is the XLA-native answer, the same construct JAX and MaxText rely on: the 94 identical layers become one compiled loop body, so compile time and program size stop growing with depth. The graph splitter is the more flexible alternative: it keeps the layers unrolled but cuts the captured step into per-layer executables, which works no matter what kind of layers you have (and does not require layers to be the same). We run both for this model and they land within a few percent of each other. Either way the activations do not fit in HBM at sequence length 4096 with 16 sequences per device, so both paths offload layer activations to host memory and prefetch them back for the backward pass.

From there the playbook applied, one change at a time, each measured on the same 64-chip slice. We raised the scoped VMEM budget so the compiler could keep more kernel intermediates on chip, which also removed an exposed update at the tail of the optimizer step. We enabled a set of libtpu scheduling flags that let XLA's latency-hiding scheduler overlap the FSDP all-gathers and reduce-scatters with the surrounding compute and offload the reduce-scatters to the SparseCores, so most of the collective time is hidden behind compute, leaving only a small exposed reduce-scatter tail in the backward pass. We switched attention to the tokamax splash kernel, and replaced the expert matmuls with specialized paired grouped-matmul kernels backed by a K-tiled weight-gradient kernel, with hierarchical reduce-scatter and the SparseCore latency-hiding scheduler to hide the expert-gradient collectives. A fused route-score backward removed a large fp32 copy from the MoE backward pass. The last round of fixes came from profiling at 1,024 chips: keeping the blocked activation layout under scan offload, raising the backward layer-scheduler threshold so the expert reduce-scatters overlap with compute again, and pipelining small reduce-scatters across the scan loop's back-edge. The recipe runs at ~32% MFU on 256 v7x chips with fp32 gradient reductions kept throughout.

We also used this model to test how far TorchTPU scales, from 64 chips up to 8,192-chip v7x pod scale, in both single-slice and multi-slice configurations. A TPU slice is a set of chips connected directly over the inter-chip interconnect (ICI); multislice lets one training job span several slices connected over the data-center network (DCN), which is how a job grows past the largest single slice. Within a slice we run FSDP over ICI, sharding parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the slice's chips; across slices the model is replicated and the gradients are all-reduced over DCN once per step, so the only traffic on the slower network is a single gradient reduction, which overlaps with the backward pass. That is hybrid sharded data parallelism (HSDP), and it is what the 2,048- to 8,192-chip runs use, with 1,024-chip slices as the sharding group. The framework behaved as expected throughout: per-chip throughput dropped by 8% going from 64 to 8,192 chips (4,568 to 4,208 tokens per second per chip), near-linear scaling across 128x more chips. One caveat: for a model of this size, data parallelism beyond about 1K chips is a scaling experiment rather than a training recipe. This is a weak-scaling run: the batch per device stays fixed as chips are added, so the global batch grows with the chip count and at 8k chips is larger than one would use to train this model. What the run shows is that the framework, the compiler and the collectives hold up at that scale, not that this is the configuration to train with.

The three case studies above are deep dives: one model at a time, with a parity test and a profile behind every change. A team arriving on TPU usually has a different problem. They have a model they already train, often a Hugging Face one, and quite likely it won’t be the model that TorchTitan ships for TPU. They may well want every last percent out of it eventually, but first they need an easy way to get it running at all. That is the problem the Transformers modeling backend solves: it builds the model from the Transformers library by its Hub id and runs it through TorchTitan's trainer and parallelism instead of its own. On TPU the backend has a TorchTPU lane with a single configuration that applies the first rungs of the playbook optimizations to any supported checkpoint, with no change to the model code: SimpleFSDP in place of FSDP2, per-block torch.compile, the splash attention kernel registered as an attention implementation with the transformers attention interface so the model's own attention calls land on it, the fused Pallas cross entropy fed the final hidden states and the head weight instead of materialized logits, and, for mixture-of-experts checkpoints, the TPU grouped-matmul experts substituted for the portable implementation. Most of the dense architectures the backend supports train this way unmodified; mixture-of-experts checkpoints run through the same path but without expert parallelism yet. None of this reaches the hand-tuned numbers above, but it is a working, reasonably efficient first run for a model that has no TPU recipe yet, and a way to find out whether it deserves one.

Sooner or later a model deserves more than a generic path: it is the one you will train for months, it has an architecture the backend cannot express, or the out-of-the-box number is not the one you need. Porting a model to a new accelerator used to be a specialist project measured in weeks, with the hard-won lessons living in one engineer's head. On TorchTitan TPU it is a repeatable procedure. The repository ships a model-onboarding skill for coding agents that captures how the case studies above were done and walks an engineer, or the agent itself, through the same ladder, with the tests, the acceptance bars and the traps built in.

The roadmap runs along five lines: production readiness, precision, hardware, parallelism and models. On production readiness, the recipes gain the operational tooling that long runs on Google Cloud expect: integration with the ML Goodput Measurement library, so a run reports how much of its chip time turns into preserved training progress and where the rest goes, and with Multi-Tier Checkpointing on GKE, which keeps checkpoints in local memory and in-cluster replicas with Cloud Storage as the durable tier, so large jobs save often and resume quickly. On precision, the float8 recipe that today ships for Llama 3 70B, built on torchao's Float8Linear and v7x's native fp8 matmuls, extends to the rest of the model set. On hardware, Google has announced its eighth-generation TPUs, TPU 8t for pre-training and TPU 8i for inference and reinforcement learning, and TorchTitan will support them as they become available on Google Cloud, with the same recipes carried forward. On parallelism, expert parallelism for the MoE kernels is the open item named earlier, and long-context training is next after it, now that million-token context windows are the norm for frontier models. On models, the targets are the next size up from Qwen3-235B: Qwen3.8-Max, a 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture of experts, and Kimi K3, 2.8 trillion parameters with Kimi Delta Attention in place of standard attention on most layers, which will exercise the kernel plug-in path as much as the scaling one.

TorchTitan on TPU is no longer an experiment. The same codebase and plain-PyTorch model definitions train Llama 3 405B at about 57% MFU on up to 1,024 chips, and run Qwen3 235B, a mixture-of-experts model, on up to 1,024 chips in a single slice. In a weak-scaling test with a fixed per-chip batch, Qwen3 235B kept 92% of its per-chip throughput from 64 to 8,192 chips. That shows the framework, compiler and collectives hold up at pod scale, even though a model of this size would not be trained at that scale. The pieces that make this possible are not buried in one recipe. SimpleFSDP, the Graph Trainer with scan and the graph splitter, host offload, the Pallas kernel library and the optimization playbook are building blocks, each behind a flag and each documented with the number it is worth. For models that TorchTitan does not ship, the Transformers modeling backend runs 500+ Hugging Face models through the same trainer with the first optimizations already applied, and for teams that want more than that, the onboarding skill turns porting a model into a repeatable procedure that an engineer or an agent can follow.

That leaves two ways to use it. The first is to adopt TorchTitan as the training framework: pick a recipe, launch it on a slice, and build on a configuration whose performance is already known. The second is to keep the training code you have and take what you need: the kernels are standard PyTorch custom ops, SimpleFSDP and the Graph Trainer are modules you can import, the compiler flags and the playbook apply to any TorchTPU workload, and every recipe spells out what it enables and why. Either way, the fastest way to find out what this does for your model is to run it.

#10495. Scientists are rethinking what menopause does to the brain. Here’s what they’ve discovered

As we age, hormones change in dramatic ways that can alter our mental and physical health—and the science around those hormones is changing too.

A new study just published in the journal Neurology sheds light on the ways estrogen may protect the brain as it ages, and the results are promising.

The research examined the health outcomes among 352 cognitively unimpaired women who underwent a brain MRI at age 70 and again five years after the first scan. Out of the group, women who had longer lifetime exposure to estrogen through oral birth control and menopausal hormone therapy showed fewer physiological markers associated with Alzheimer’s disease and had healthier brains overall.

Scientists have already established a connection between longer reproductive spans—basically, the number of years after menstruation starts and before it stops—with reduced brain aging later in life. That research and other findings suggest that estrogen has a strong neuroprotective effect, basically working as armor for the brain against cognitive decline. But as women age, their estrogen levels begin to decline, lowering the hormonal barrier that protects the brain during the body’s reproductive years.

Giving the brain a boost

Estrogen supports cognitive health in a number of ways, including reducing inflammation, boosting blood flow, and protecting the brain’s white matter—the connective tissue that works as a superhighway between neurons.

“The long-term impact of endogenous and exogenous estrogen fluctuations on late-life [cerebral small vessel disease] severity remains poorly understood,” the paper’s authors wrote. That condition is associated with cognitive deterioration and Alzheimer’s, a devastating disease that is almost twice as common in women as in men.

“Previous studies have linked longer reproductive span, earlier [periods], and later menopause to reduced brain aging, reinforcing the neuroprotective role of estradiol,” the authors wrote. “While longer lifetime estrogen exposure may provide neuroprotection, abrupt estrogen loss may increase neuropathology accumulation and dementia risk.”

The new research is important because it shows a link between external or “exogenous” sources of estrogen and improved brain health. While doctors can’t dictate how long a person’s brain might be protected by naturally occurring endogenous estrogen, exogenous estrogen can be sourced from oral medications (including birth control pills), transdermal patches and gels, injections, and topical creams.

A changing story about estrogen

The conversation around estrogen has been in the midst of a seismic shift.

A year ago, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration initiated the removal of black box warning labels from hormone-based drugs used to treat perimenopause and menopause symptoms.

The stern safety warning was first put in place more than two decades ago, cautioning clinicians and causing panic among patients that estrogen-based drugs could raise the risk of serious medical issues, including heart attacks, blood clots, and breast cancer. For years, that official guidance prevailed, in spite of evolving research showing that many patients can benefit from and use these medications safely.

In response, estrogen is undergoing something of a renaissance. More people are talking openly about what they experience during menopause and perimenopause (the hormonally chaotic phase before the body fully moves into menopause). For many women, those hormonal changes crash into their personal and professional lives with an array of mood and physical symptoms that go well beyond hot flashes.

The changing discourse has been a boon for telehealth providers like Midi as a whole generation of women explore the fact that a simple patch, pill, or gel might boost their quality of life considerably.

“With few exceptions, there may be no other medication in the modern era that can improve the health outcomes of women at a population level more than hormone replacement therapy,” former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary said last year, extolling the long-term benefits of hormone therapy as “tremendous.”

The promise of relief for symptoms like brain fog, hot flashes, depression, and anxiety has been enough to drive a nationwide shortage of estrogen patches. As new research delves deeper into the ways that estrogen may protect the aging brain, many women will have one more reason to hit up their doctor for a chat about hormone therapy.

#10492. How Applicant Tracking Systems Read Resumes: 7 Checks Developers Should Make

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A resume that looks perfect on screen can look like a pile of scrambled text to a program. Applicant tracking systems (ATS) and hiring tools do not see your layout. They extract text from a file, guess where the sections are, and store what they find. If that step fails, the best experience in the world never reaches a human reader.

This matters whether you are sending your own resume or building a tool that processes thousands of them. This article walks through seven checks you can make with a few lines of Python, including one script you can run today.

A resume is a document with no guaranteed structure. One person writes "Work History", another writes "Experience", and a third uses a two-column layout that reads out of order. Any tool that processes resumes first has to turn this into predictable fields: contact details, sections, dates and skills.

Thinking in terms of a target schema helps. SitePoint's article on JSON schema design for document AI shows how the structure of the labels you define determines whether a document pipeline works. The same idea applies here: decide which fields you need before you write any extraction code.

Do not judge a resume by how it looks. Judge it by what comes out when you extract the text. SitePoint's walkthrough on building a JSON dataset from PDF documents describes a pipeline that extracts text from PDFs and then cleans up common extraction artifacts. That cleanup step exists because raw extraction is rarely tidy. Read the raw output first, and note what is broken.

PDF files store where characters are placed on a page, not what they mean. The pypdf documentation on extracting text from a PDF says this directly: there is no semantic layer, spacing is hard to get right because text is absolutely positioned, and pypdf is not OCR software, so it will never extract text from images.

Two practical results follow. A resume saved as a scanned image has no extractable text at all. And fancy layouts such as columns, text boxes and tables can come out in the wrong order.

Once you can extract text, a short script can catch the common failures. This one reads a PDF and reports whether it contains text, whether an email address is found, and which standard sections are missing:

Run it on a resume and look at the result. If has_text is false, the file is probably an image. If sections are missing, check whether your headings use unusual names. A passing result does not prove that every ATS will read the file the same way, but a failing result is a clear warning.

Different tools parse differently, so one script is only one opinion. A resume writing service such as ResumeCroc lists a free ATS resume checker among its tools, which is a quick way to see how another tool reads the same file. The linked page is a commercial service page, and every ATS behaves differently, so treat any checker as one data point and compare it with your own extraction results.

Most extraction problems come from layout. Single-column pages, standard headings, plain fonts and real text instead of images give parsers the best chance. Avoid putting contact details in headers or footers, since some tools skip them. If you are building a parser, test files with columns and tables on purpose so you know how your tool fails.

Create a folder of sample resumes: a clean one, a two-column one, a scanned one and one with unusual headings. Run your check against all of them whenever you change your parsing code. This turns "it seems to work" into something you can verify, and it makes regressions obvious.

Do all applicant tracking systems read PDFs the same way? No. Parsers differ in how they handle layout, headers and tables, so test more than one file format and more than one tool.

Is a Word file safer than a PDF? Not necessarily. Both can parse well or badly depending on layout. Test your own file instead of assuming.

Can a script guarantee my resume will pass an ATS? No. A script can find obvious problems, such as missing text or headings, but each hiring tool has its own rules.

Hiring tools read text, not layout. Define the fields you care about, extract the raw text first, understand what PDF extraction cannot do, automate basic checks, compare with an outside checker, keep formatting simple, and test against a small set of sample files. The script above is short, but it moves the question from "does it look right" to "what does a program actually see".

#10488. Apple is slashing AI budgets—the latest company to do so

Tokenmaxxing is on the way out, even as some of the biggest players in the tech industry are urging their employees to use AI as much as possible. A new Bloomberg report reveals that Apple is cutting employee budgets for AI token usage while remaining just as committed to deploying AI to boost efficiency. 

Apple has already reduced the daily spending limit from $300 to $200 for certain engineers, according to Bloomberg, but the company reportedly plans to cut that down even more. Sources told Bloomberg that the daily cap could drop as low as $100 for some engineering teams. In many other departments, daily AI spending is already capped at $100; now Apple is considering reducing the limit to $25 for certain teams. 

The spending limit is measured in tokens, which are units of AI usage that represent fragments of text or data processed by AI systems. 

This move comes as Apple continues pressing its engineers and other employees to use AI more in day-to-day operations. But it also reflects a larger trend rippling across the tech industry, as companies struggle to justify their outsize spending on artificial intelligence. 

After pushing their employees to adopt AI, many tech employers seem to be grappling with the fact that those investments have not yielded the productivity gains that they anticipated. 

According to Bloomberg, some Apple employees believed many people weren’t making use of the $300 limit and that it was higher than needed. But other employees seemed to view it as a sign that Apple is looking to reduce costs—and that the company could resort to layoffs. 

Bloomberg reports that Apple is already taking steps to streamline its operations in the interest of maximizing efficiency, and recently appointed CEO John Ternus is reportedly already advocating for reducing layers of management (something that Amazon has also sought to do over the last year).

There are plenty of signs tech companies are tightening their belts, even as they continue to prioritize AI adoption across their workforce. Uber exhausted its annual AI budget in a matter of months, leading the company to cap monthly spending at $1,500 for each AI coding tool. Companies like Meta, Microsoft, and Tesla have all imposed token limits on their employees. 

Beyond AI spend, however, the fear of layoffs looms large across the tech industry. 

A steady stream of employers have trimmed head count in the last year due to AI investments, either to offset exorbitant AI spending or because AI has enabled them to cut back on certain jobs. A number of companies, including Microsoft, have given their workers the option of taking a voluntary buyout, presumably to stave off job losses or avoid the negative attention associated with major layoffs. 

As Fast Company reported this week, some workers have even started to worry about AI being used to select employees for layoffs as companies shed jobs and reshape their workforce. In other words, it seems companies are continuing to demand more of their employees, but with less support—human or otherwise.

#10486. How to Quickly Check What Your HTML Code Looks Like in a Browser

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Writing HTML is one of the main parts of building a website. It is mainly responsible for webpage structure and content.

A small error can result in layout problems. Oftentimes, you don't notice these issues until you preview the page in a browser. A quick way to ensure that your layout looks the same as you want is to preview your HTML code.

In this blog, we’ll show you easy ways to check how your HTML code will look in real time. So keep on reading till the end.

The following are two easy ways to check how your HTML code will look in real time.

This is a simple way to preview your HTML. You don't need a web server to preview your HTML code. You have to follow the following steps.

Open a code editor or simply Notepad on your device. Create a new file and paste your HTML inside it.

Step 2 - Save the File With an HTML Extension

After adding your HTML code in Notepad, save the file as index.html. You have to ensure that the extension is .html, not .txt.

If you are using Notepad on Windows, click on “File” and navigate to the “Save As” option and click it. Then enter index.html as the filename. Make sure that Notepad doesn’t save it as a text document.

Locate the saved file on your device. Double-click to open it in your default browser. The browser will render the HTML elements to show the headings, paragraphs, and buttons on the page, as you can see in the image below.

This is how you can create a simple file to preview your HTML before deploying it. If you see any errors, you can correct them in your file and preview it again.

However, it is worth considering that HTML may not show the complete website behavior alone. The final result can also depend on JavaScript, external CSS, or other resources. You should check those files as well.

This method provides an easy way to preview your HTML code. It involves using a specialized online HTML viewer. This approach is even quicker and doesn't even require you to create a local file first.

Step 1 - Open the HTML Viewer Open your web browser and search for an HTML viewer. You may see multiple tools in the search results. Select one that allows HTML preview online. For demonstration purposes, we are using HTML Viewer by minifier.org.

Once you’ve selected the tool, open it. Navigate to its input box and paste your HTML code into it. We are using the same HTML code from the first example.

You can also upload your file or paste its URL into the tool. After entering your HTML code, click on the “View” button to preview your HTML code.

In the screenshot above, you can see the tool showing the HTML preview on the right side. This tool also gives you the option to edit your HTML code and see the results in real time through the “Auto-update” option.

If the auto-update option is checked, you can see the changes in real time as you edit the code. This makes editing much easier, as you can modify the code and preview the changes immediately without returning to your original file. It also allows you to verify how your layout will appear on desktop, tablet, or mobile. You can check this by clicking on the icons provided in the top right corner of the tool. Once you are satisfied with the output, you can copy or download your edited HTML file easily.

This tool also allows you to test the HTML code of your game or video in real time, as you can see in the screenshot below.

These features make such specialized HTML viewers practical. These are quick and easy to use. However, the features shown above may not be available on all the tools. If you are specifically looking for such features, you can read the tool’s description for these features before using it.

HTML is one of the main components of a website. It defines the structure and content of webpages. Many users need to check how their HTML code will look in a browser to identify potential issues before deployment.

To preview your HTML code, you can use simple methods. One is to paste your code into Notepad and save it as index.html. Then open it in your browser to get a preview of your HTML code.

You can also use a specialized HTML viewer. Such tools can work by just pasting the code into the input box. Once you paste your code, click on the view button to get a preview of your HTML code. Some tools also offer various other features, such as editing, viewing games, and videos in real time.

Both of these methods work fine. The choice depends on the user's preferences and needs.

#10485. The midterm elections’ blue wave could throw a wrench in SpaceX’s mobile ambitions

Elon Musk has made no secret of his hopes of turning SpaceX into a viable competitor to mobile companies like Verizon and AT&T. But with the Democrats’ resounding victory in the 2026 midterm elections, that plan is suddenly thrown into question.

SpaceX has been busy over the past month making deals and positioning itself to step into the mobile space. In October, it bought an 800 MHz spectrum portfolio from private equity firm Grain Management, which had acquired it from T-Mobile following its 2020 merger with Sprint. And earlier this week, SpaceX struck a deal with Qualcomm to build out base stations for its planned mobile carrier. Taken together, those moves bring the company closer to entering the market.

But to launch the new division, SpaceX will also have to jump through legislative hoops, something that could be significantly more challenging with the Democrats in charge.

Several Democratic candidates made it clear they planned to target Musk—who spent $500 million trying to stop the blue wave—should the party gain a majority in the midterms.

Some lawmakers want to explore potential conflicts of interest in the billions of dollars Musk’s companies receive in federal contracts and subsidies. Others have questions about his possible role in throttling internet access to Ukraine’s army. And several want to do a deep dive into Musk’s role at DOGE (the Department of Government Efficiency that he spearheaded)—which accessed tremendous amounts of sensitive data.

Last December, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Democratic Representative Greg Casar of Texas began warning about SpaceX’s possible entry into the mobile market amid a proposed deal to acquire some wireless spectrum licenses from EchoStar.

That deal, they wrote at the time, “would help Musk expand SpaceX’s Starlink capacity and provide an opportunity for the company to gain ‘firepower’ in the satellite communications industry that competitors will struggle to compete with. . . . The close relationship of Mr. Musk to the Trump administration and to key Trump administration officials make it particularly important that the FCC and DOJ engage in a robust, independent, and impartial review.”

The deal, valued at $17 billion, ultimately went through.

Building a network

SpaceX didn’t stop there. Last month’s purchase of the 800 MHz spectrum portfolio seemed mundane at first glance. That frequency was used by Sprint to power its push-to-talk/walkie-talkie-like features in 2004. SpaceX, though, saw it as a way to bypass building an expensive, complex network of repeaters across the U.S. and the globe, when used in conjunction with its Starlink satellites.

“Starlink’s satellite signal at 2 GHz can reach your phone outdoors, but it dies at the first wall,” wrote Aakash Gupta, a product management leader, creator, and educator in a post on X. “800 MHz penetrates buildings. Most phones already have the band built in. So satellites handle the open sky, this low-band layer handles indoors, and suddenly Starlink Mobile covers everywhere a normal carrier does without the tower network.”

Musk was similarly upbeat, writing on X that the portfolio is “the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America.”

The deal with Qualcomm will enhance the cellular infrastructure and enable high-capacity coverage for Starlink Mobile. There are even reports SpaceX is in talks to buy Boost Mobile or use its network, which would give Musk another entry into the mobile market.

Allies and advantages

Come January, Musk will have significantly fewer friends on Capitol Hill—and many more enemies.

“We must get big money out of our politics, so no billionaire or trillionaire can buy our elections,” James Talarico, the Democratic Senator-elect from Texas, said in his victory speech. “We must unrig this economic system that only benefits the top 1%.”

Musk does have one powerful card up his sleeve, however. His relationship with President Donald Trump, which has been rocky in the past, is on solid footing once more, and Trump still controls executive agencies, including the Federal Communications Commission, which could help SpaceX’s entry into the market.

Timing could also play to Musk’s advantage. Verizon’s CEO has estimated it will take at least four years for SpaceX to become a viable player in the market. Musk claimed it would take half that time, but it’s worth remembering he has a history of being overly optimistic in his timeline forecasts.

Whether it’s two years, four years, or more, the past few elections have shown that, politically, a lot can change in that span.

#10483. Inside the jagged era of AGI: 5 key takeaways

Below, Kevin Roose shares five key insights from his new book, The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence.

Roose is an award-winning technology journalist, bestselling author, and cofounder of Machine Gods Media. He previously spent a decade as a technology columnist for The New York Times, where he co-created and cohosted the popular podcast Hard Fork. He now cohosts Machine Gods, an AI-focused podcast produced in partnership with NPR.

What’s the Big Idea?

For years, the world’s leading AI researchers have raced to build a technology that many of them fear. But the finish line keeps moving as AI becomes more capable. The truth is, we’re already living in the early, imperfect years of artificial general intelligence, and our institutions are dangerously unprepared for what comes next.

Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Roose himself—in the Next Big Idea app, or buy the book.

1. The people most afraid of AI are the ones building it.

This is, in some sense, the founding paradox of the whole AGI story. You’d assume the people building AI are true believers who expect it will do amazing things, like cure cancer and end poverty. And some of them are. But a surprising number of key figures in this race got into AI because they were terrified. They read the arguments about what a superintelligent machine might do to humanity, took them seriously, and concluded that if this thing was going to be built no matter what, it had better be built by people who were scared of it and would take the appropriate precautions.

Ultimately, I came to think of the AI world as having three tribes. There are the scientists, who see AGI as the ultimate intellectual challenge and want to use it to discover new drugs and cure disease. There are the seekers, who see it as an evolutionary turning point for our species. And then there are the survivalists, who think that if this technology isn’t built by the good guys, then the bad guys will do it instead.

The trouble is that getting there first is what everyone is trying to do. And they all end up concluding that the only way to move forward responsibly is to accelerate. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, left OpenAI partly out of concern that it was moving too fast, and then went on to build a competitor that had to move just as fast to stay ahead. He’s living inside the paradox, and so are many of the people in this book.

2. The secret was a big blob of compute.

For most of AI’s history, smart people assumed building an intelligent machine would require understanding the human brain, writing down the rules of reasoning, and encoding knowledge the way you teach a student. But what worked instead was almost embarrassingly simple.

Amodei outlined it in a 2017 paper he called “Big Blob of Compute.” Essentially, you take a neural network, feed it enormous amounts of data, and then throw a huge computer at it. The model then learns to recognize the patterns in that data the same way a human toddler does, by looking at a lot of examples until it clicks.

Amodei called this his Big Blob of Compute hypothesis, and it reoriented OpenAI’s research away from narrow applications and toward a more general approach. It’s what led to GPT-1, GPT-2, and ultimately to the large language models that we use today. This simple recipe is the engine of everything that follows.

3. Feeling the AGI is a key ingredient in AI progress.

In San Francisco, people talk about “feeling the AGI” as a kind of spiritual awakening that comes from living on the technological frontier, internalizing the enormously fast pace of progress, and building up to something unimaginably vast. The people who work at these companies believe that they are building something closer to an alien species than a product, and they treat their work as a humanitarian mission: deliver AGI safely into the world before someone else screws it up.

“Feeling the AGI” is what Ilya Sutskever, the former chief scientist of OpenAI, called this feeling. He’d stand up at company gatherings and lead chants. He burned effigies. “Don’t lose sight of what we’re actually building here,” he said. “This is not a tool. This is something more like a being.”

Feeling the AGI is now pretty common. It’s why we see researchers from AI companies speaking up about their fears and why lawmakers and regulators are desperate to slow down this industry. But for many years, the people feeling the AGI were few and far between. They worked at a handful of small AI companies that were little known to the general public. And they shared this secret which led them to double down on their research. The people who felt the AGI early won. They became the people who now run some of the most powerful companies on Earth.

4. There is no finish line.

For years, everyone in the race to AGI operated under the unspoken assumption that the race would eventually end. The idea was that someone would train an AI model that was clearly as smart as the smartest humans. That person would walk out on a stage and say, “We have built AGI!” And the race would be over.

Some leaders even started making plans for after AGI. Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, mused about handing over control of the company to an AGI and finding some hobbies for himself. Demis Hassabis, former CEO of DeepMind Technologies, told friends he would take a yearlong sabbatical and wander the gardens in Princeton, New Jersey, the way Albert Einstein did. Dario Amodei wanted to spend more time at his family’s farm in Italy with his favorite horse, Calypso.

But around 2025, I started hearing a different phrase in AI circles. They called this the Red Queen’s race. It comes from evolutionary biology, via Lewis Carroll, where the Red Queen tells Alice that it takes all the running you can do just to stay in the same place. That’s what the race to AGI has become. Nobody agrees on what AGI is or how we’ll know that we’ve achieved it.

Every time one company ships a breakthrough, the others match it within months, and the goalposts get moved again. At Google, Larry Page, the cofounder who had been thinking about AGI longer than almost anyone, reportedly told people he would rather see Google go bankrupt than lose the race. Meanwhile, other Google executives were saying that AGI was still five years or more away. And the CEO, Sundar Pichai, was barely using the word at all.

Everyone in AI is running as fast as they can, and nobody is getting anywhere relative to each other. So unless this changes, or we slow the whole thing down, the post-AGI future of garden strolls and hobbies and Calypso the horse will have to wait.

5. AGI is here, whether we feel it or not.

By the definitions of AGI that people in 2016 were using—a machine that can do most cognitive tasks about as well as most humans—I think we’ve already gotten there. Today’s AI models can write, code, analyze documents, pass professional exams, solve unsolved math problems, and tutor children. If you went back in a time machine with a laptop and a copy of ChatGPT or Claude to 2017 or 2018 and showed them to a thousand of the leading researchers in the field, they would not have hesitated to say this is obviously AGI.

The reason that it doesn’t feel like AGI is that this intelligence is jagged. AI systems are superhuman at some things and bafflingly bad at others. They can solve the Riemann hypothesis or disprove the Jacobian conjecture and then miscount the letters in a word or fail at basic arithmetic. That unevenness makes it easy to dismiss them. You just find the one thing they can’t do and conclude that it’s all hype.

But a jagged intelligence is still an intelligence. In some ways, our human intelligence is just as jagged. I’ve come to think that the useful definition of AGI isn’t about capability. It’s about generality: a single system that can be pointed at almost any problem and make real progress on it. By that standard, we’re not waiting for AGI to arrive. We’re living in the early, awkward, jagged years of it.

One of the biggest risks I see isn’t a robot uprising. It’s a world where the technology has already changed, and the institutions in charge of our society—governments, companies, schools, and communities—keep acting like it hasn’t. The people in this book have been feeling the AGI for years. Now it’s time for the rest of us to catch up.

This article originally appeared in Next Big Idea Club magazine and is reprinted with permission.

#10480. Amazon controls its delivery drivers. NYC wants it to employ them, too

Every workday, Luc Rene puts on a shirt and pants branded with Amazon’s logo and heads to a distribution center, where he climbs into a van that also carries Amazon’s logo across its side to deliver packages with the company’s swoosh smile emblazoned on them. When he rings customers’ doorbells, he yells out, “Amazon.”

But Rene is not technically an Amazon employee. He’s employed by a delivery service provider (DSP) that contracts out his labor.

That could soon change in New York City, where Rene lives and works, if the City Council passes the Delivery Protection Act. The bill would require companies like Amazon to directly employ the people who deliver their packages while also creating a licensing system that would hold the companies to new safety, training, and labor standards. It has the backing of Mayor Zohran Mamdani and 31 of the council’s 51 members—enough for it to pass if brought to a vote. Supporters of the bill say it would increase street safety while also providing better protection for the workers who deliver Amazon packages.

Amazon has lobbied heavily against the bill. “We’re committed to creating good jobs and supporting our thousands of employees in New York City. We’re equally committed to the local small-business partners who work with us every day to provide fast, reliable delivery for New Yorkers,” Amazon spokesperson Steve Kelly tells Fast Company. “But as written, this legislation would directly undermine that commitment—threatening the small businesses that deliver to customers, putting the jobs of more than 5,000 of their employees at risk, and forcing us to consider relocating delivery operations outside of the city.”

Safety on the job has been an issue for Rene ever since he started delivering Amazon packages in 2022. After completing a training on a computer, he was supposed to spend a day being trained by an experienced driver; the driver never showed up, so Rene drove by himself. Since he was never told how to avoid injury during his shifts, which stretch 10 or more hours, he’s come up with his own regimen, stretching before and after work.

“No driver is ever required to complete a delivery if conditions aren’t safe—and neither they nor their DSP is penalized for making that call,” Amazon’s Kelly says. “Any allegation of unsafe working conditions would be taken seriously and we investigate accordingly.”

In 2023, Rene slipped and injured his knees while delivering a package. Unsure whether he could access Amazon’s medical services, he called his employer, which asked only whether he could keep working. He did, despite the pain, taking painkillers to get through it. “If I can’t show up to work due to the pain, I won’t get paid,” he says.

His experience appears to be common: A 2025 report from the New York City comptroller’s office found that last-mile facilities like the DSP that employs Rene reported an average of 678 injuries per year from 2022 to 2024, and 85% of them were severe enough to keep people from working or to need a reassignment. Amazon’s DSP program had the highest injury rates.

In response to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the New York Delivers coalition, which represents DSPs and is bankrolled by $5 million in money from Amazon, says DSPs “provide flexible, good-paying jobs with strong workplace standards, opportunities for career advancement, and competitive benefits,” adding that the Delivery Protection Act “effectively eliminates the small businesses in the industry, and puts over 10,000 New York City jobs at risk.” Amazon also paid to bus in workers and DSP owners to oppose the bill in a city council hearing earlier this year.

“On paper, Amazon’s not my employer”

When Rene started driving, all he and his fellow drivers were given to haul packages, some of which weigh more than 40 pounds, were giant plastic bins called totes. He says it took a strike in 2024 and a march on their boss to get hand trucks. The effort of dragging totes across the ground left Rene with back pain that lingers today.

There are other health and safety issues. In the summer, the heat is “really painful,” he says. But two years ago, Amazon instituted a change that means when he exits his van, the air-conditioning shuts off, leaving the van to bake while he makes his deliveries. The DSP has no control over that, he says, nor over how many packages he’s expected to deliver in such conditions.

In fact, Amazon directly controls much of Rene’s workday. When he shows up to the DSP, he has to hope Amazon provided enough routes for him to actually work that day; otherwise, he gets sent home. He must be in full company uniform before even leaving the dispatch center to get in his van. Once he arrives at the van, he has to go through an inspection checklist created by Amazon before he can drive the vehicle. If a defect is found, it’s Amazon that decides to ground the van, and the DSP has no power to override the decision, Rene says.

Further, Rene says Amazon dictates how much time he gets to load up the van before facing a penalty. Kelly denies that Amazon controls workers’ schedules, saying, however, that it does “assign dispatch windows.”

Cameras inside the delivery van watch Rene’s every move during his shift—and it’s Amazon, not the DSP, that watches the feed. (Kelly asserts that the cameras are only for safety and not for productivity or performance tracking, although many reports have disputed that.) If Rene presses the accelerator or hits the breaks too hard, Amazon gives him an infraction. If he gets into an accident while driving a delivery van and calls the DSP, he’ll be forwarded to an Amazon representative.

“On paper, Amazon’s not my employer, but in reality, Amazon is,” he says.

For all of this, Rene makes $25 an hour—a figure he arrived at only after a recent 25-cent raise that was implemented by Amazon. If the Delivery Protection Act passes, it “would change everything, honestly,” Rene says. Although he’s a member of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters union, the act would allow him and his fellow delivery drivers not only to unionize but also to negotiate directly with Amazon.

Then they can demand better training, higher pay, health insurance (especially critical for workers injured on the job), more control over their schedules, and a guaranteed 40-hour workweek. “All those little things to make the job feel, not easy, but basically like I can show up to work today and I know I’m safe,” he says. “Make it feel like I have something reliable, something people can actually live on.”

#10478. AI Testing Tools: Benefits, Limitations, and Best Practices

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every vendor says the same thing: buy our AI, and testing gets easy. Don't believe it. AI testing tools do help, though. Some teams save real hours with them, while others waste a quarter and a budget. The difference usually comes down to how they start.

They support your QA team by writing test cases, running them, spotting failures and suggesting repairs. Some tools read a requirements document. Others watch real users click around and then replay what they did. Playwright, for instance, now ships built-in test agents: a planner that explores your app and writes a test plan, a generator that turns the plan into test files, and a healer that runs the suite and tries to repair failing tests.

Old-school automation needs a person to write every script. Then a developer moves one button and the whole thing falls over. Somebody loses a morning to repairs, and QA engineers hate that part of the job.

Quality is the big worry. Generated tests can look clever and prove nothing. A tool might confirm that a checkout page opens and then mark checkout as covered, but opening a page is not testing it. Even Playwright's documentation says generated tests may contain initial errors and that you should review what the healer changes before accepting it. A person has to read the output every time.

Business logic is the next problem. The tool has no idea that your refund window dropped from 30 days to 14, and it cannot feel that a signup form is confusing. Intent lives in people's heads.

Coverage numbers can mislead. A dashboard says 90%, and the room relaxes. Meanwhile, the odd edge cases nobody thought of sit untouched. Bugs do not read dashboards.

Check fit first. Does it cover web, mobile and API tests, and does it work with your stack? Ask before any sales call, not after. Then test its honesty: when something fails, a good tool tells you why. A vague red mark costs your team time because nobody can verify it. Read the pricing page slowly, too, since some vendors charge per seat and some per test run.

Finally, throw your ugliest feature at it. Demos use tidy little apps, but your product has pop-ups, slow pages and odd corners. Watch how the tool handles those.

Expecting instant results. People switch the tool on and wait for magic. What they get is noisy reports and grumpy engineers. Some managers even cut QA headcount right away, which is a bad idea: somebody has to tune the tool and handle the cases it cannot. Good testers become more valuable, not less.

Skipping training. Your team needs to learn how the tool behaves. Two short workshops and a shared doc go a long way.

Trusting machine-written text without a second look. AI tools now draft test descriptions, bug reports and release notes too. If your team wants to know how much of a document was machine-generated, an AI-content checker such as ZeroGPT can give a rough signal. Treat the result as a hint rather than proof, because such detectors make mistakes and publish their own accuracy claims.

Agents are the obvious next step. Instead of running fixed scripts, they poke around your app like a curious user, clicking, typing and reporting anything strange. Early versions already exist, and they are rough but improving.

Editors will change as well. Your code editor may soon suggest a test the moment you finish a function, and some bug reports may arrive with a fix attached. The wall between development and QA is getting thin.

Yes, but carefully. AI testing tools will not replace your QA team. They take the boring work off testers' hands and spot patterns people might miss, but they still need a human to say "that result is wrong." Start small, measure what happens and keep your testers close to the tool. Do that, and you will ship faster without losing control.

#10476. Give your products an annual review

I spent the first half of my career as the product manager at a software company. Product teams are constantly reviewing their products, assessing: What do our customers want? What changes should we make? Do we (maybe) need to retire a product altogether because it no longer serves its purpose?

Most solopreneurs don’t take the same approach. They continue to push the same products or services, or tack on new items until they have a large suite of offers they have to maintain. We rarely take anything away.

I’ve gotten into the habit of an annual review to make sure everything I put out into the world for my business still makes sense for both me and my customers. 

The trap of adding and never subtracting

Part of the joy of running a solo business is launching something new. You get to make all the decisions about what an offer looks like and how to launch it. 

Removing an offer is a lot less fun. It can feel like a loss. Plus, you may have material (website, slide decks, email sequences) that need to be updated.

The problem is that every offer needs upkeep. Content gets out of date. You may also be paying for tools related to hosting or delivering an offer that isn’t doing anything for you. 

I create a lot of resources for solopreneurs, often describing systems or processes that make a solo business run efficiently. These can quickly feel dated—or even obsolete—as technology changes. 

For a long time, I spent my precious hours creating new resources without a process for updating existing material. That’s a mistake, since outdated information quickly erodes trust.

The questions I ask about every offer

Now I take time to review every product and service I offer and ask myself the same questions:

Is anyone buying it? I start with sales or bookings from the past year. Low numbers aren’t automatically a reason to cut, but I need to review the offer more closely.

Do I still want to do this work? A service can sell well and still be work you don’t enjoy.

What does it cost me to maintain? I count the time I spend updating information and supporting it, plus the time it takes to promote. Then I add any tool subscriptions tied to it.

Does it still fit where my business is headed? An offer that made sense two years ago may not match the clients or work I want now. 

I maintain a business road map and value statements, and compare my offers against these documents. I use AI to help this process by having Claude do the initial comparison. This becomes my checklist for a human review and assessment.

What to do with an offer that isn’t working

Keeping an offer as is and cutting it aren’t the only two choices. There are a few other paths:

  • Refresh it: Update outdated content.
  • Reprice or repackage it: Raise the price or bundle it with something else so it doesn’t stand on its own.
  • Re-promote it: Sometimes there’s nothing wrong with the offer; perhaps it just hasn’t been marketed enough.
  • Retire it: Take it down, and let existing customers or clients know if needed.

I have a resource related to AI tools for solopreneurs. It made sense when I first created it several years ago. Now it’s impossible to maintain because the AI changes at lightning speed. Instead of spending my time updating it, I spent my time finding all the places where I reference this resource and removing it.

But to start, the most important step is making the time for a review. Block off time on your calendar once a year or put it on your to-do list. The review process is separate from acting on your decision. Your goal is to land on “Where do I go from here?”
