#10474. How the country’s tallest mural was painted onto the side of this NYC building

In the South Bronx, residents can now look up to their heritage—literally.

A new mural by the Dominican artist Néstor Omar García, who also goes by the name Angurria, climbs 29 stories high on one tower in the Morrisania Air Rights public housing campus. It fills the skyline with a colorful take on a neighborhood block party crowded with children, elders, and, yes, even a DJ.

Titled Un MAR de Gente / From Every Shore, the artwork is said to be the tallest mural in the U.S., transforming an otherwise dull concrete facade of the brutalist New York City Housing Authority building into a public artwork.

The project was spearheaded by the New York City-based nonprofit ArtBridge and the strategic consulting firm FOGA. Support came in the form of grants from Public Housing Community Fund and MAC Viva Glam, the line of lipsticks that helps fund community causes. For a little over a year, the organizers worked alongside the artist and the community to complete the artwork.

“Hundreds of windows face this wall—neighbors, schools, offices—so everyone can enjoy this mural from their windows,” says FOGA’s founder, Fernando Ortiz.

Stacked into three sections that blend into one another, the mural collages three interconnected stories into a single scene. The top section symbolizes how older generations pass down knowledge to younger ones. To depict this, Angurria painted his “Doña Patria” character—a woman wearing hair rollers that he based on his mother and frequently returns to in his work—carrying a child on her shoulders.

The middle section features a party scene, with seven people wearing common emblems and fashion from the neighborhood. One dons the borough’s “X” symbol on a hat while an elder with a beard sports a Knicks cap and an orange tracksuit. In the corner, a young woman wears a hijab and Yankees jersey.

The bottom section shows two children playing around an open fire hydrant, which represents the past and the innocence of childhood.

The entire artwork was conceived of collaboratively with the community. FOGA organized six workshops with South Bronx residents to gain their input. Together they voted on artist they wanted to make the mural, the bright color palette, and the symbols and motifs that would be depicted, like hip-hop and sports teams.

After deciding on the mural’s nonnegotiables, the group passed the list to Angurria, who would then return with design concepts. They traded ideas and feedback until they were all happy with the result.

The mural is 307 feet tall, and the scale serves a purpose. “We look down at our phones so much and public art forces you to look up,” Jon Souza, program director at ArtBridge, tells Fast Company. Like the mural’s main figure who is looking upward, Doña Patria, passersby need to look up from their phones and up to the sky to view the whole work.

“You can’t experience the mural without doing the same,” Souza said.

Installing a mural at the scale of a 29-story building involved careful logistical planning. Just three artists painted it.

Many murals are first traced using a projection, but due to the size of the wall, that was not possible here. So Angurria turned to virtual reality (VR) instead. Using measurements from the building’s blueprints, he mapped out the final design to scale and divided it into sections, assigning a corresponding pattern to each floor.

Angurria and an additional artist then jumped on a swing scaffolding lift—the kind window washers use—and traced the virtual pattern, visible through the VR headset, onto the facade. Just laying down the figures’ black outline took around one full day. Next, they applied acrylic paint, then latex; they finished the details with spray paint. The entire process took 22 days.

The mural has become a conversation piece. Community members who contributed to the project proudly point out how their ideas are now part of the cityscape. That, more than the mural’s monumental size, is the greatest outcome as far as the organizers are concerned.

“We set out to create the mural without knowing the record-breaking scale it would ultimately reach,” Souza says. “But the scale, attention, and recognition it received have only amplified the sense of pride and ownership around the project.”

Angurria, though not part of the Bronx by birth, was embraced by the community as a result of the mural. On the artist’s birthday, which landed on one of the 22 days spent painting the piece, neighbors brought him cake and coffee.

“He is the artist who did the mural, but now he is also family,”  said Ortiz, the FOGA consultant.

#10473. Google shuts down a sneaky malware backdoor on millions of Android TV and Google TV boxes

Google has confirmed that an Android TV device maker snuck a backdoor for malware onto certified devices, which is leading to security improvements for the ecosystem as a whole.

In a post today, Google confirmed that it has cut ties with “Videostrong,” a company that was manufacturing certified Android TV boxes. This is due to the company building in a backdoor that it could sell access to, including the distribution of malware. Google has taken legal action to block the domains and servers that “Videostrong” was using to control the XCPE botnet and malware modules and banned the company and its subsidiaries from selling certified Android devices going forward, or selling software to any other certified vendors.

We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

Synthient (via The Hacker News) compiled a list of potentially affected devices, with the focus being on the Mecool brand that has made some well-known Android TV and Google TV boxes in the past. Mecool has been rumored to be shutting down.

Google somewhat admits that this was a failing on its part, as these devices were sold as “certified” Android devices with the implication that they were safe. The company explains that these bad actors “employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device’s first boot.” With that in mind, Google is updating its review process to protect users against this type of behavior, and Google reiterates that “a device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust.”

Google’s shutdown of the domains and servers used to spread malware should leave affected Android TV and Google TV boxes safe to use – the company says that “taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices” – but owners may still want to consider alternate options.

#10472. ‘War’s painterly, kinetic title sequence is a boxing-inspired knockout

To capture the feelings of polarity, conflict, and tension in the title sequence for War, the HBO legal drama about a fictional, high-stakes divorce case, designers created an animation that captures conflict through clashing colors.

Imaginary Forces, the acclaimed production studio behind title sequences for Stranger Things, Mad Men, and the 2026 Milan Cortina Games, as well as War, wanted to express the visceral nature of the show’s namesake in a way that felt abstract and impressionistic. To do that, they used black, white, and red paints animated in splotchy, splattered, and kinetic brush strokes that move like they’re battling on screen. Considering the characters’ extreme wealth, the idea of playing with art to do that felt like a natural way to show it.

War is set in London and stars Dominic West as the founder of a fictional social media site, Zephyr, and Sienna Miller as his wife, a movie star whose new film is a period drama called The Milliner. Their ensuing divorce descends, as the title suggests, into an all-out, winner-take-all battle.

“We did a lot of tests internally,” Ronnie Koff, creative director at Imaginary Forces, says of the creative development process. After starting with physically painting on glass, they pivoted to digital paint brushes on the Procreate iPad app so they could iterate faster. Initially, they were inspired by the mid-twentieth-century expressionist Franz Kline, who painted abstract brushstrokes to capture emotion through line quality and positive and negative space. But that didn’t really get at the feeling Imaginary Forces was going for.

“At the very beginning it wasn’t working,” Koff tells Fast Company. “My challenge was, how do you take something that is purely abstract where you just get an emotion from it, and give it a literal, almost anthropomorphized quality where it feels like there’s tension through the animation that you create.”

Koff’s team eventually began referencing boxing as a way of establishing the look of a punch and counterpunch between two opponents, and the title sequence shows those boxing-inspired movements to suggest the idea of a fight. The color palette is mostly black and white to quickly communicate the idea of opponents, with a red accent color to add a visceral quality, he says.

The paint strokes also have a three-dimensional, physical texture that Koff says is inspired by the scratch board quality of the 1996 title sequence for Se7en, directed by Kyle Cooper, which became the catalyst for his cofounding of Imaginary Forces three decades ago this year. That title sequence showed the potential for creative intros that contribute to a show’s narrative, but these days, technology can make that harder than ever to accomplish.

“One of the things that I’m always up against is the skip button,” Koff says. “How do you engage people in a way that feels a little different, so people aren’t immediately clicking that? And so my first thought is to really present something a little different, something that might be a little unusual but could grab your attention at the same time.”

By animating painterly brushstrokes with an aggressive physicality, War‘s title sequence commandeers a symbol of wealth—fine art—and transforms it into an emotional visualization of combat.

#10471. The Meta Quest 2 and Quest Pro are receiving their last OS updates soon. Here’s what you need to know

The best-selling VR headset of all time (and its Pro-level cousin) will no longer receive OS updates after March 2027.

Somehow, the Meta Quest 2 has been around for six whopping years, and Meta is finally bringing support for the headset to a close after March 2027. The far less popular Meta Quest Pro, which uses the same chipset as the Quest 2, will also see OS updates cease at the same time with OS v213. Meta will continue to deliver security updates through the end of 2027 to both headsets, according to an official Meta developers blog post.

Meta says it will not be removing cross-play multiplayer functionality or blocking access to Quest 2 players, so any games that support the headset will continue to work after these dates, so long as they don’t rely on any new OS features introduced after March 2027. Developers have to give players a 6-month notice if support is ending for a game, so you’ll have ample time to decide what to do.

That means the Quest 2 will receive just over 7 years of total security updates, while the Quest Pro gets two years less (since it came out in October 2022). The Meta Quest 2 remains the best-selling VR headset of all time, with around 20 million units sold over the lifetime of the headset. Meta says that Quest 2 owners can still play games throughout this time, although game support will likely dry up quickly after January 2028.

The $599 Meta Quest 3 and $349 Meta Quest 3S, which debuted in 2023 and 2024, respectively, are the follow-ups to the Quest 2. The upcoming Meta VR Glasses, which will retail for $1299, feature a next-generation chipset, a significantly higher-resolution AMOLED display, and substantially lighter weight and smaller size than either Quest 3 model.

Meta VR Glasses are expected to debut early next year, and with them, a new generation of OS development will take place. Since the Quest 2 uses a significantly outdated mobile chip at this point, it makes sense for Meta to cease new feature development for it and focus on newer, more capable hardware.

#10469. ‘Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness should be reflected in our computing systems’

Is this our Golden Age? One where

we are free of our labors

and joined back to nature,

returned to our mammal

brothers and sisters,

and all watched over

by machines of loving grace

(excerpt from a poem by Richard Brautigan)

More than a decade ago, I began to engage in a series of wonderful philosophical discussions with Julio Frenk (then the president of the University of Miami, now the chancellor of UCLA). From our talks an idea emerged, a fusion of computing, technology, political systems, philosophy, economics, and governance. We manifested some of the thinking in Project Alexandria (2018) and with a Knight Foundation Grant (2022): Conversations on the Future of Democracy, Social Media, and Artificial Intelligence in the Americas.

I was planning to go back to school and work on a PhD in Philosophy on this thesis—what we called “computational democracy”—and was greatly discouraged by a philosophy professor at one of the schools where I applied: “Go build it, don’t be a philosopher; this is too important.” So I did, and I founded SynthBee with the core idea that we would be the rebel alliance, the Jedi (not the Sith) and a north star in the ideals of computational democracy.

What President Frenk and I conceived was more than a philosophy. It was architecture, system design, use, and operations of certain types of computing and intelligence systems manifested from the idea of personal freedoms. The idea of computational democracy in many ways reflected the ideals of liberty and the checks and balances of a well-run democracy.

Looking back, the Bay Area of the late 1960s and 1970s was a hotbed of these ideals, in many ways birthing a mix of music, film, creativity, and technology. Stewart Brand’s DIY Whole Earth Catalog (which influenced the internet and the web), the Homebrew Computer Club, and the birth of personal computing with the Apple I were all markers of this fusion of freedom, democracy, and computing. The Grateful Dead played a key role, encouraging a blend of audience and band, fan participation, and the birth of open sharing. The ideals of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness could, and should, be reflected in our computing system architectures and design.

Distribution of power

Today, the core philosophy of computational democracy includes the distribution of power and decentralization, strong protection of users and their IP and data, and systems designed to be safe and trustworthy by design (not by hopes and wishes). Of even higher importance is the ideal of empathy for humanity, and of placing people in the center. I look back at what we built at Mako Surgical, which helped to define the field of collaborative robotics, or Cobots, deployed in operating rooms around the world. And I see in those systems—their behavior, their connection to the surgical teams and patients—the emerging principles of computational democracy. 

I would argue and hope that Richard Brautigan would have seen the glow of a machine in true loving grace in the symbiosis between human and machine that exists with surgeons and the Mako robot, and the good they bring to patients. (Fun fact: The Mako robot was deeply influenced by R2-D2, and the love and good R2-D2 brought to the Star Wars world.)

The alternative

On the other end of the spectrum lies computational autocracy: massive, centrally controlled computing platforms run by a few techno-oligarchs who wish to amass and control all the world’s computing power, data, intelligence, and IP.

The scaling and financial performance of these companies has created techno-monarchs. And in turn, actual monarchs, dictators, and autocrats have deeply immersed themselves in the creation, acquisition, and interweaving of these systems in how they govern, control, and suppress their populations. The cozy interplay between technology dictators and actual dictators has blurred the line between technology and government, with both sides fusing and enriching themselves.

The ideals of absolute control, central power, and asymmetrical economics are deeply embedded in a large number of companies chasing the idea of artificial general intelligence (AGI), a form of techno-deity right off the pages of any classic Marvel or DC villain comic. Shall we play a game? With the whole world?

The rest of us are meant to be the serfs, living upon the lands of the manor lords, who harvest and gather us as produce and commerce. Computational autocracy maintains a manifest belief in the manor lords’ power, their right to rule, their right to take our data, our IP, and our work.

AGI is a very hungry ghost, and it demands nuclear power plants, endless computing power, a lack of ethics, and a willingness to be blind to the chaos, hallucinations, danger, lack of trust, lack of testability, and unknown intentions of these massive machines and their owner overlords. And of course, catastrophic or existential risks to humanity (but who cares when we upload to the Great Cloud on Mars?)

Humanity, all of us, is at a fundamental crossroads (the Robert Johnson kind). We can surrender thousands of years of hard-fought struggle to overthrow oppressive kings, queens, emperors, dictators, and madmen—to live freely and to find our purpose in life, to improve the world, and to self-govern (for the people, by the people). We can throw that all away and hope and pray and believe that the mighty few will somehow care for us with their even mightier machines, and we shall become subordinate to their immense wealth and near-endless power.

Or.

We can live in a Golden Age, a neohumanist renaissance where our computing systems and machines reflect the ideals of liberal democracy, personal liberty, safety, trust, and the sovereignty of your data, your creativity, and your inventions.

Choose well. Our world and future depend upon it.

#10467. National Nacho Day 2026: Here’s a list of deliciously cheesy freebies and deals

Serious question: What do you call cheese that isn’t yours? Nacho cheese, of course.

Thankfully, the queso and more can be yours if you celebrate National Nacho Day, which is today (Friday, November 6, 2026). Before we get into where to get the best deals, let’s look at the history of this delicious dish.

A brief history of nachos

Nachos were an invention of necessity. In 1943, Ignacio “Nacho” Anaya García was employed at the Club Victoria restaurant in Piedras Negras, Mexico.

When some American military wives from just over the border in Eagle Pass, Texas, took a day trip, they stopped by the restaurant. Anaya wanted to offer them refreshments, so he fried some corn tortillas and topped them with cheese and jalapeños.

Nacho’s new dish was an instant hit.

He opened his own establishment, El Nacho, in the 1960s, which helped spread this new culinary delight. A recipe was published in 1954.

Nachos came to Los Angeles via El Cholo Restaurant and a waitress named Carmen Rocha.

A processed pourable cheese became a staple ingredient in the 1970s, thanks to a Texas businessman, Frank Liberto.

This forward thinker first sold nachos at Arlington Stadium, where baseball’s Texas Rangers once played. This action cemented the dish’s popularity with sports fans.

These days, nachos are as unique and versatile as the person who makes them.

National Nacho Day freebies and deals

It’s time to get even cheesier than our opening joke. Let’s see where we can chow down on some nachos.

At participating Moe’s Southwest Grill locations, rewards members can enjoy $5.99 nacho entrees beginning on Friday, November 6 (National Nacho Day) through Sunday, November 8.

On the big day at participating Las Palapas locations, the friendly staff wants you to have something to wash down your nachos with. This chain is offering 50% off on full orders of bean and cheese nachos and $5 regular margaritas.

Another half-off deal is going down at participating Condado Tacos locations. You can choose where you consume them; the offer is good if you dine in or order online. It even comes with free delivery if you order through November 8, spend at least $30, and use the Condado Tacos app. Talk about options.

If you find yourself near Nashville, head to El Comal Mexican Restaurant for 25% off all nachos.

In Pleasant Hill, California, east of Berkeley and Oakland, Cantina Jack’s is offering happy hour nacho pricing all day long.

However the tortilla chip crumbles, we hope it’s deliciously cheesy.

#10466. Testing JSON-LD Like an API: 7 Checks Before Your Next Release

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A content editor changes an article’s headline. The page updates immediately, but its JSON-LD still contains the previous title. A redesign introduces a new author component while an old plugin continues publishing a different author name in the page source.

Neither failure necessarily produces a JavaScript error. Both leave machines and readers with conflicting descriptions of the same page.

For developers, the useful approach is to treat JSON-LD as a maintained output of the application, with a data source, validation rules, and regression tests. This guide uses a blog template to show how. You will need basic JavaScript knowledge and a modern Node.js installation for the runnable tests.

Requests for search improvements often arrive as broad outcomes: improve discoverability, clarify entities, or support answer engines. These need to become implementation requirements before development starts.

For example, AEO directory includes structured data within descriptions of broader optimization services. For an engineering team, the actionable deliverable is a page representation whose types, properties, and values can be checked against the published content. I personally used this , and adding this because this can help other developer's and designer for optimization and get higher search result's.

For a blog template, define these acceptance criteria:

Keep implementation success separate from search outcomes. Google’s AI features guidance says there is no special Schema.org markup required for its AI search features. Correct markup also does not guarantee rich results or inclusion in an AI-generated answer.

Avoid separate, manually maintained copies of the headline, author, and publication date. Both the visible template and metadata builder should consume the same published record.

Save the following as article-schema.mjs. The builder assumes an upstream content-validation step has already checked required strings, timestamps, and approved HTTPS URLs.

This is a deliberately small example, not a complete rich-result eligibility checklist. Add relevant images and other supported properties when the real page supplies them. Consult the Schema.org BlogPosting definition and Google’s Article documentation for their respective vocabularies and search guidance.

Use a consistent canonical-URL policy before building the identifier: normalize the intended hostname, trailing-slash convention, and query parameters. Do not generate a fresh UUID for the same article on every request.

SitePoint’s guide to implementing JSON-LD on modern websites covers embedding approaches across common stacks.

Valid JSON is not automatically safe to insert into a raw HTML script element.

A CMS value containing can terminate the element at the HTML-parser level, even when the value belongs to a JSON string. Concatenating a headline directly into a script tag is particularly risky.

Append this helper to article-schema.mjs:

JSON serialization handles quotes and backslashes. Replacing literal less-than characters prevents an embedded closing-script sequence from appearing in the resulting text. The Next.js JSON-LD guide documents this approach for script embedding.

Use the serialized result as the content of a script element with type="application/ld+json". Follow your framework’s documented embedding mechanism so the JSON is neither double-encoded nor inserted through an unrelated HTML context.

This helper is specific to JSON-LD script content. It is not a general-purpose HTML sanitizer, URL validator, or substitute for validating CMS data.

The tests should catch changes that would make metadata misleading or unsafe, not merely confirm that an object exists.

Save this file as article-schema.test.mjs beside the builder:

These are unit tests for the builder and serializer. They do not prove that a template embeds the script correctly or that the deployed page is eligible for a search feature. SitePoint’s explanation of unit, functional, and integration testing helps distinguish those responsibilities.

A passing builder test cannot detect a page component reading a different CMS field.

Add a browser-level check against a controlled article fixture. Inspect its visible heading, byline, dates, canonical link, and JSON-LD together. For this template, assert that the intended article entity appears once and matches those visible fields.

Do not assert that the entire page contains exactly one JSON-LD script. A site may legitimately publish organization, breadcrumb, and article entities separately. Instead, identify the relevant entity by its @id and detect conflicting definitions.

Include these failure cases in the test plan:

Prefer generating metadata from the content loaded during server rendering or static generation when that fits the application. If it is injected client-side, inspect the rendered result and test navigation explicitly. Avoid making essential metadata depend on a user interaction.

No single tool establishes syntax, semantic accuracy, search eligibility, and content consistency at once.

Test both representative code samples and deployed URLs. A validator cannot confirm the truth of an author name simply because the property is syntactically valid.

Google’s general structured-data guidelines also require markup to represent the page accurately. Treat validation warnings as findings to investigate; do not add invented reviews, dates, or attributes merely to improve a tool’s output.

Ownership matters after the first release. Decide which application layer generates article markup, who maintains its mapping, and which publishing events invalidate cached output.

When an editor changes a headline, the visible page and JSON-LD should be rebuilt or refreshed together. Updating one while serving the other from an older cache creates a mismatch even if both implementations are individually correct.

Avoid setting dateModified to the current time on every deployment. A CSS update or infrastructure rebuild does not necessarily mean the article changed. Read the timestamp from the editorial record instead.

Before shipping a template change, run the builder tests, inspect one rendered page per affected template, and check representative deployed URLs. Keep a small fixture set that includes optional fields, long text, translated content, and script-like strings.

A reliable JSON-LD implementation has a traceable relationship with published content. When someone changes the page, its machine-readable description should change predictably—and the test suite should expose the cases where it does not.

#10464. Innovation starts at the edges

Most products, services, and systems are designed around a composite of the “average” user. That sounds logical. If you are trying to serve the largest possible market, why wouldn’t you design for the middle?

The dilemma is that the composite often fails to reflect how people actually live or experience the world. Those differences can expose where products, services, and systems work well, and where they do not.

Design innovation comes from many places. Accessibility should be one of them. It is a powerful lens, revealing friction, hidden assumptions, and opportunities that are easy to miss when we design only for the middle. Solutions developed for people who face the greatest barriers can make products better for the mainstream as well.

DESIGN AROUND CONSTRAINTS

Consider the familiar examples. Curb cuts were initially introduced to make sidewalks accessible to wheelchair users. They now also serve people pushing strollers, travelers with luggage, and workers moving carts. Closed captions are essential for people who are deaf or hard of hearing, and useful in noisy airports and quiet offices. Voice controls can be indispensable for someone with limited dexterity and convenient for anyone whose hands are occupied.

OXO, the maker of Good Grips kitchen utensils, offers a compelling business example. When founder Sam Farber saw his wife struggling to use a conventional vegetable peeler because of her arthritis, he recognized an opportunity to rethink an everyday product. The resulting Good Grips utensils—with their comfortable, easy-to-hold handles—addressed limited dexterity while appealing to consumers of all abilities. What began with one person’s difficulty became the foundation of a successful mainstream consumer brand.

These examples show how designing around constraints can lead to simpler, more intuitive solutions. The benefit need not stop with the people whose needs first inspired the design. A product that is easier to operate with one hand, or a service that eliminates unnecessary steps, can improve the experience for many more people. The implications extend beyond individual design decisions. Looking at familiar problems through the experiences of people whose needs have been overlooked can challenge conventional thinking, generate entirely new ideas, and reveal opportunities that might otherwise remain invisible.

Those opportunities may go well beyond improving existing products. When companies look closely at needs that are not being met, they may discover markets they have overlooked. What initially appears to be a narrow market can reveal broader demand and inspire new products, services, or business models. That is an opportunity to rethink what the mainstream market really includes, rather than assuming that existing customers represent everyone who might benefit.

A DIFFERENT APPROACH TO INNOVATION

Realizing that potential requires a different approach to innovation. Accessibility needs to influence the choices made at the beginning, when companies are defining the problem and imagining the solution. That means involving people with different needs and abilities in those early decisions, rather than asking them to assess a product after its basic design is settled. Their perspectives can challenge assumptions and reveal possibilities that might otherwise remain invisible. The aim is not to develop a separate product for every circumstance, but to build a richer understanding of what good design can accomplish.

There is another reason this matters now. Populations are aging. Expectations around independence and participation are changing. More customers expect products and services to fit the ways they live, rather than requiring them to adapt to rigid systems. What once seemed like a niche need may point to a much larger opportunity.

The edges of the market are moving closer to the center.

For business leaders, the choice is not between designing for accessibility and designing for the mainstream. That is a false distinction. The real opportunity is to make accessibility part of the thinking that shapes products and services from the outset. Meet needs that have too often been overlooked while creating something more useful for a broader population.

The best design begins by asking who has been left out of the design in the first place.

Gail Zauder is cofounder and CEO of AbleFly.

#10461. Without your audience in the room, your brand is guesswork

A group of experienced executives is discussing how the brand can “connect with Gen Z.” Everyone has a deck and an opinion. But nobody in the room is Gen Z. I’ve sat in this type of meeting more times than I’d like to admit.

We collect demographic reports, analyze trends, and increasingly ask AI to tell us who our audiences are and what they want. But this goes wrong when we allow it to replace conversations.

A generation is not a community. A community is not an individual. People born in the same years can have almost nothing in common beyond their age. Demographics describe groups, not the individuals within them.

I’m more interested in what they choose and why. What do they dedicate their time to? Where do they gather? Why do they feel like they belong there? You cannot design your way into cultural relevance without first understanding the culture.

FEELINGS INSTEAD OF DATA

Pep Salazar has spent more than two decades learning this lesson from another perspective. As cofounder and director of OFFF, the international creativity and design festival that began in Barcelona over 25 years ago, he has helped turn a gathering of digital creatives into an enduring international community.

When we spoke recently, Pep described the tension between knowing an audience through metrics and understanding it as people. Sponsors want attendance numbers, engagement reports, and evidence of reach. Those figures do offer important insights, but they don’t explain why someone travels to Barcelona to spend three days among fellow creatives.

For him, it’s more interesting to understand feelings rather than data. A dashboard can tell you what people clicked. A conversation can tell you why they care.

Pep wants people to spend time together and talk. But his approach goes further. He also learns by taking risks. Pep deliberately introduces new perspectives and ideas that challenge what his audience already knows and expects. Not everything resonates immediately, but that’s part of the process. As he puts it, “I understand by doing.”

UNDERSTAND BY DOING

That’s an important distinction for brands. Understanding your audience doesn’t mean always giving people more of what they already know and love. It means knowing when to experiment and introducing something unexpected. And learning from the response.

When inviting a target audience into the process, you don’t have to outsource every decision to them. You can develop the judgment to understand when to respond to a community, and when to challenge it with something unfamiliar.

Pep also points to another common mistake brands make when trying to connect with creative communities: Don’t show up only to sell. He has watched brands arrive at OFFF with polished corporate messaging, while missing the social dynamics of the event. His advice is simple: “Come here to understand the people and to talk to them.”

LANGUAGE AND SOUL

He also worries that generative AI is making corporate language more interchangeable. “When you speak similar to your neighbor, then you don’t have a soul,” he told me.

I recognize that problem from my own work. Too many brands begin by studying the competition and end up borrowing its language, aesthetics, and assumptions. The result may look professional, but it rarely feels personal and unique. People want brands with personality that speak the language of their community.

So the next time people in a boardroom start debating how to reach a particular audience, ask who is missing in the room. Invite your audience in before the strategy is set in stone. Spend time where they gather. Make room for opinions and responses that might contradict your brief and give those perspectives the power to change the outcome.

Otherwise, the empty chair at the table says more about your brand than the strategy deck ever will.

Erik Herrström is founder and creative director of STUDIO HERRSTRÖM.

#10460. Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU

As part of our broader announcements for PyTorch today, we are excited to launch native PyTorch backends for vLLM (developed in partnership with Inferact) and SGLang (developed in partnership with RadixArk).

For years, TPUs have powered large-scale AI workloads with high performance and efficiency. With the rise of agentic and multimodal workloads, serving efficiently is more important than ever. Both engines already run on TPU through JAX-based backends, but we kept hearing from developers that they wanted to customize and debug their serving stack in PyTorch.

So we started in earnest on TorchTPU, which runs PyTorch natively on TPU. We then built new vLLM and SGLang engines on top of it.

Our goal is for the PyTorch community to bring models to TPU and make them fast using the tools developers are already familiar with. The engines come with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels.

Serving at scale requires co-design across every layer of the technology stack, from silicon to compilers to orchestration. Today's launch of new inference engines is at the central part of an integrated, open TPU ecosystem.

TorchTPU makes the TPU a native PyTorch device. Tensors are managed as standard PyTorch tensors on a tpu device with no wrapper types, code runs eagerly or compiles via torch.compile using XLA, and collectives go through torch.distributed.

Because each device runs its own PyTorch process, both engines keep each framework’s worker model, scheduler, KV cache manager, API server and so forth, with TPU implementations underneath.

Most models use the standard upstream PyTorch model definitions in both engines, with TPU-specific optimizations in kernels and layer implementations. Custom kernels written in Pallas are called directly from PyTorch as custom operators inside the compiled graph. This platform-plugin design reuses as much of each framework as possible while letting TPU optimizations move at their own pace.

Both engines are built for the full range of production workloads.

Agentic workloads in particular demand several of these features simultaneously. Because agents repeatedly resend expanding multi-turn conversations, serving them efficiently requires finding the cached prefix instead of recomputing it. Both engines keep reusable prefixes in HBM and, with host offload turned on, automatically move older prefixes to host memory as a second tier.

Two of these features move the KV cache away from the device that computed it. Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate TPU hosts, so each request's KV cache has to travel from the prefill host to the decode host.Tiered KV offload moves the part of the KV cache that no longer fits in HBM to the host's DRAM and secondary storage with Google Cloud Managed Lustre, and brings it back when a later request reuses the prefix. Either way, the transfer has to overlap computation or it adds directly to latency.

Both engines use TPU Sync for this. It is an open-source C++ library for KV cache transfer and management on TPU. It reads the device buffers behind PyTorch tensors directly, so a transfer needs no extra staging copy on the host, and it runs transfers on its own threads outside Python while prefill and decode continue. vLLM-TorchTPU exposes it through vLLM's KV connector interface. SGLang-TorchTPU uses it as a disaggregation transfer backend and as the I/O backend for HiCache.

Both engines are already running at scale in production with preview customers. To provide transparent, reproducible proof of our performance, we benchmark in public through the community-standard SemiAnalysis InferenceX project.

Building on our initial submission of Qwen 3.5 on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), our engineering teams have further optimized the stack, bringing the lowest cost per million tokens overall to an industry leading 2.01 cents. Alongside these improvements, we have also published new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance results to AgentX, the project's dedicated track for evaluating agentic long-context and multi-turn workloads. Ironwood TPU leads across most of the Pareto frontier. We look forward to continuously updating our public performance profiles as we bring more models and configurations to the leaderboard.

We did not build these backends in a vacuum. By embracing PyTorch and working directly with open-source project maintainers, we ensure these engines remain upstream-aligned and community-first:

This partnership is bringing SGLang's stellar team to build for TPU, delivering an engine that is already running in production at Meta and battle-tested at scale across demanding real-world scenarios.

Together, we integrated a high-performance Pallas megakernel for the 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3 model that runs the entire decode step as one kernel, serving more than 700 tokens per second to a single user on Ironwood TPU. Building on this work, Inferact recently led our first preliminary AgentX submission for Kimi K3 on the vLLM-TorchTPU stack. This initial milestone already demonstrates exceptional performance per TCO in ultra-high-interactivity workloads, and the rapid increase in the maturity of the vLLM and PyTorch ecosystem on TPU for doing new frontier OSS models bring-up, with follow-up submissions set to unlock even greater efficiency through larger scale prefill/decode disaggregation.

To foster continuous open-source contribution, vLLM is also launching a first-of-its-kind community contribution TPU capacity pool to provide free TPU compute to developers who actively contribute to the vLLM engine.

As the models get larger, we are evolving both engines to make large-scale TPU inference deployments performant and efficient. The major features for production-grade agentic workloads are already supported. More performance optimizations and advanced features are under way – open a Github issue to request collaboration on yours!

Across the two engines, most of the popular open model families are supported, including Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, GPT-OSS, Gemma and more. The team is investing in making more models available to run natively on TPUs, including Day 0 support for new open models. We also want to give the community the tools and TPU capacity to tune performance for their own workloads and configurations.

vLLM-JAX and SGLang-JAX remain important projects. Both will continue to be maintained, supported, and available for the community to use and adapt.

#10459. Why diagnostic delays cost more than time

The cost of delayed diagnosis in rare disease is often measured in years. It should also be measured in dollars, clinical capacity, and missed opportunities for better care.

Rare disease affects 1 in 10 Americans, and on average, the diagnostic odyssey for a patient with rare disease costs over $220,000 in avoidable medical fees and lost income. It’s significant time and money that patients and families can’t afford to lose. And it doesn’t end there.

The downstream economic impacts are also costly. Every prolonged diagnosis can trigger a cascade of additional appointments, referrals, and procedures that consume resources. Rounds of tests, specialist bottlenecks, and administrative burden intensify the longer a patient goes without a diagnosis. This reduces clinical capacity and extends wait times for patient care.

Currently, patients often navigate years of uncertainty before accessing information that could meaningfully change their care. That model is increasingly difficult to justify.

This is why a genome-first healthcare system is so compelling. A genome-first approach, where whole genome sequencing (WGS) is used as a first-line test and not a last resort, is helping redefine personalized care for patients with rare diseases. For me, this is where the field is headed. Starting with the genome gives us a more complete view from the outset. When combined with other data, it may bring us closer to answers that many families have been waiting too long to receive. It’s about using technology with purpose to move care forward for patients seeking answers.

PUT COSTS INTO PERSPECTIVE

Here’s an example of how costs may be lowered with whole genome sequencing. Consider a six-year-old with a history of uncontrolled seizures and global developmental delay. A brain MRI and EEG were performed when the child was six months old and again at three years old. These did not provide answers about his symptoms. It wasn’t until he had WGS at age six that he tested positive for a genetic change that explained his symptoms. He has SCN1A-related seizure disorder. That diagnosis provided the clarity needed to personalize his treatment plan and transform his long-term care, including both medication and dietary changes.

In this example, the total estimated costs for just the main tests performed were $12,800. Repetitive testing costs can add up fast, and it can be particularly discouraging when the testing results are uninformative. Had WGS been offered earlier in this patient’s journey, the estimated savings would have been approximately $8,900 in testing costs alone. But we also can’t forget other costs not captured here, such as medications, specialist appointments, and potentially avoidable emergency visits and hospitalizations. These additional costs can compound quickly over time.  

THE WGS BENEFITS

Increasingly, healthcare systems should question if they can afford not to use WGS earlier.

The potential benefits of doing so in patient care are clear. It can help shorten the diagnostic odyssey, minimize repetitive or uninformative tests, enable more informed medical management, and lower long-term health costs. An earlier diagnosis can also inform targeted testing for family members to understand any symptoms they may have or their own risk for that condition.

For healthcare providers and health systems, WGS can improve operational efficiency by streamlining diagnostic workflows, ultimately helping clinicians make more informed decisions sooner and minimizing unnecessary testing rounds. In acute care settings, particularly neonatal and pediatric intensive care units, rapid WGS (rWGS) can accelerate clinical decision-making and shorten hospital stays. This can generate meaningful cost savings while improving patient outcomes.  

In fact, a recent study found that rWGS as a first-line test is likely to significantly reduce the cost of acute care in a private payer system. The analysis estimated a reduction of $5.8 million to $7.8 million in inpatient payments due to rWGS results and avoided inpatient days.

Every industry eventually reaches a point where a long-standing process no longer fits its purpose. Healthcare is approaching that moment with diagnostics for rare disease. A system built around sequential testing and years of uncertainty is increasingly being challenged by a model that starts with a more comprehensive understanding of the patient. I believe the organizations that embrace that shift will be better positioned to improve outcomes, reduce waste, and deliver a more efficient patient experience.

Kengo Takishima is chairman and chief executive officer of Baylor Genetics.

#10457. Android gaming is having a renaissance

Good morning! Today I’m mourning the loss of Patrick Stewart by rewatching First Contact, my favorite Trek movie; beginning a marathon listen of at least one great Star Trek podcast; and replaying Elite Force and Armada, both wonderful Trek games released in 2000.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

I’m starting this edition of Inbox a bit later than I’d like, but for a good reason: I got swept up by the subject I was researching. See, I wanted to write about the seeming renaissance of gaming on Android, which has always had clear advantages and disadvantages compared to iOS. On the plus side, its openness bred experimentation and a healthy indie gaming scene, along with a thriving emulation ecosystem born of its ability to sideload apps and gain access to Android’s underlying file system. On the downside, its device and OS version fragmentation has kept some developers from attempting challenging console and PC ports, and led others to abandon their titles to bugs and time.

But thanks to a confluence of factors, as well as form factors, Android gaming is in a very good place right now. Despite Google’s continued ambivalence towards paid and premium games, the platform has received official ports of console hits like Dredge and Sifu, with others like Replaced, Absolum, and Dispatch coming soon. (One could argue things have been good for a while with Stardew Valley, Dead Cells, Balatro, Slay the Spire, and Vampire Crawlers available already, but I digress.)

Most of these games are embracing a try-before-you-buy model to avoid the upfront cost that so many mobile users resist, while others, like Dispatch, are getting a mobile optimization that reorients the experience for a portrait display.

And while traditional emulation has existed since Android was young, recent months have seen considerable improvement in breadth and performance, aided by AI coding tools and a community that wants to play its library of Steam, Windows, and Switch games on phones. This rabbit hole is extensive and varied: WinNative combines work from Winlator Bionic and Pluvia to run Windows games on Android and connect PC storefront libraries. DroidDeck aims for a SteamOS-like experience, putting Steam’s Big Picture interface on supported Android hardware with Windows games running through ARM64 Proton, which debuted recently with the Steam Frame.

It’s via DroidDeck that I whiled away a couple of glorious hours on my Galaxy Z Fold 8 playing Lumines Arise, a game perfectly suited to the pick-up-and-play nature of smartphones (though it’s best with a controller). The latest Qualcomm chips have long outpaced the mobile games they’ve been asked to power, but few knew just how well they’d run demanding PC and console titles, even through compatibility layers like Proton.

Similarly, an Android branch of the increasingly popular nxnative, which compiles Switch and Switch 2 games for iOS and macOS, has been making it easy to play games like Super Mario Bros. Wonder and Metroid Dread at 60fps on many recent Qualcomm-powered devices. There’s even a Switch 2 version in the works for Android.

The big question is whether all of this works well: will people spend more time arguing with the software than playing the games themselves? And on the legal side of the business, will publishers find success selling discounted versions of AAA titles on Android now that the translation tools are better and the device compatibility much broader?

If there’s one thing I’ve learned covering Android for nearly 20 years, it’s that the community always finds a way.

ICYMI: Ben’s Weekender essay is all about how Motorola is filling the gap OnePlus left behind, mostly.

The strangest thing I’ve seen recently is the rumor that Elon Musk wants to launch a Starlink-branded terrestrial wireless carrier in the US. Now we know how he plans to do it: by purchasing Boost Mobile from EchoStar and leveraging its contracts with AT&T and T-Mobile along with new low- and mid-band spectrum Starlink recently acquired. That infrastructure, combined with Starlink’s existing array of LEO satellites, could make for a compelling advantage over the incumbents: namely, that dead spots practically won’t exist anymore.

But as we’ve learned from countless examples over the years, running a low-margin, high-churn postpaid wireless business is not for the faint of heart, and I’m not sure why Musk has decided that now is the right time to do it.

Five years on, is the Pixel 6 series really the disaster that we remember it being? The answer, according to Damien Wilde, is a bit more nuanced.

The Pixel 6 and Pixel 6 Pro were fundamentally flawed pioneers for Google. They were the firm’s most ambitious hardware undertaking to date, and simultaneously one of the most frustrating phone series to live with during their initial launch window and beyond. If the Pixel 5 was a safe play ahead of this big pitch, the Pixel 6 was a risky dive into deep waters. It stumbled badly. Yet without those painful growing pains, the more polished, confident, and reliable Pixel devices we enjoy today simply would not exist.

Finally, networked supermarket freezers in Sweden, Belgium, and Luxembourg were hacked over the weekend, sending temperatures up to a reported 50 degrees Celsius, and all the food inside them straight into the trash.

According to Reuters, “The latest incidents follow an attack in France last month when police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses.”

What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented. As we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carry-in inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. For the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs…Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase.

John Ternus, Apple CEO, during the company’s Q4 2026 earnings call

Thanks for reading, and have a great day. I’ll talk to you on Thursday.

#10456. Denny’s store closures: See a list of shuttered locations as another franchisee files for bankruptcy

The fate of dozens of Denny’s restaurants is hanging in the balance after a long-struggling franchisee for the beloved diner chain sought Chapter 11 protection on Wednesday, the latest in a string of bankruptcies involving a once-sprawling restaurant empire owned by a former McDonald’s executive.

The franchisee, EYM Diner, operated roughly 30 Denny’s restaurants at the time of its bankruptcy petition on Wednesday. A number of its locations had already closed in the lead-up to the filing, some quite recently.

Denny’s has been working behind the scenes to help keep the remaining restaurants open, the brand tells Fast Company.

EYM’s bankruptcy follows a lawsuit last month by one of its lenders, InterBank, which claims to be owed more than $18 million, and which has been pushing to have the restaurants sold to a more “capable” operator. 

Citing inspections from Denny’s, InterBank’s lawsuit documents an extensive period of alleged operational decline for EYM, claiming the conditions at its restaurants are “poor and getting worse,” including “food safety conditions at several locations that would likely not pass muster with the health department.”

“Denny’s cannot permit the operation of a substandard restaurant without damage to its brand,” the lawsuit states.

A lawyer for InterBank did not respond to a request for comment.

With restaurants located across Texas and Florida, EYM and its affiliates this week sought protection from bankruptcy court in the Northern District of Texas.

The franchise is owned by fast food entrepreneur Eduardo Diaz, a former president of McDonald’s Mexico, whose various companies have filed for multiple bankruptcies in recent years, Restaurant Business reported.

Diaz did not respond to requests for comments.

The embattled entrepreneur previously operated Pizza Hut, KFC, and Panera Bread locations, including several that reopened this year under new ownership, as Fast Company previously reported.

Mark Burgess, Denny’s chief development officer, told Fast Company in a statement that the diner chain has worked with Diaz for two years to try to sell the restaurants. That effort is still ongoing.

“There are viable restaurants in this group, and franchise partners within our system are willing to step in to help secure their future,” Burgess said.

Which Denny’s restaurants have closed? 

According to a franchise disclosure document issued by Denny’s in April, Diaz operated 39 Denny’s locations as of the end of last year.

Some of those stores have since shuttered. A Fast Company review of the addresses revealed at least eight Denny’s locations affiliated with Diaz that have been marked as closed on review platforms or delivery services.

Texas

  • 2655 Grapevine Mills Cir E, Grapevine, TX 76051
  • 510 W Lyndon B Johnson Fwy, Irving, TX 75063
  • 6480 N Fwy, Fort Worth, TX 76137

Florida

  • 3701 Bee Ridge Rd, Sarasota, FL 34233
  • 5603 E Hillsborough Ave, Tampa, FL 33610 
  • 1245 N Atlantic Ave, Cocoa Beach, FL 32931
  • 255 E Altamonte Dr, Altamonte Springs, FL 32701
  • 4390 US-27, Sebring, FL 33870

The locations appear to have closed recently, with reviews for some of the stores appearing as recently as this week.

As of Friday, the locations have either been removed from Denny’s store locator tool, have been marked as not accepting orders, or have phone numbers that appear to have been disconnected.

It was not immediately clear if any of the locations could reopen at some point.

Specific Denny’s closures were not mentioned in EYM’s bankruptcy petition, though a typical course of action would be for the company to ask for court permission to get out of its lease obligations following the bankruptcy.

The above list of store closures may not be complete. We’ll update this story if we learn of more.

Why does all this sound familiar?

This is not the first franchise bankruptcy to impact Denny’s in recent months. In September, franchise owner M15 Inc. closed several Denny’s restaurants in Minnesota and Wisconsin in the lead-up to a Chapter 7 bankruptcy filing.

Denny’s Corporation, which was taken private and delisted from the Nasdaq earlier this year after years of struggles, is now in the hands of private equity backers. As of the end of last year, the chain had 1,274 locations, most of which were franchise-owned.

#10452. Google’s Ocarina of Time easter egg is a blast from the past

If you’re sick of AI search and all the business of modern Google search, this week’s Google easter egg will take you back 28 years to a simpler time when Ocarina of Time was the pinnacle of gaming, and Google was still a new name.

It’s hard to believe I was sitting on a couch in my parents’ living room 28 years ago, playing Ocarina of Time on my Nintendo 64. Apparently, the folks at Google feel just as nostalgic as I do about the upcoming release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo Switch 2.

Case in point, if you go to Google right now and search for “Zelda” or “Ocarina of Time,” you’ll see a Master Sword appear in the bottom-right corner of your screen. Tap that sword, and you’ll be magically transported back to the way Google looked back in 1998. It’s just seven blue links with short descriptions on a very simple page. Even the “I’m Feeling Lucky” button works!

Unfortunately, the theme only works for this specific search, so you can’t keep things looking retro if you search for anything else, even if you start from the old-school search box on the 1998-themed page. Bummer. Tapping the Master Sword again brings you back to 2026 Google search, complete with a great little animation and sounds of Link in adult or child form, depending on which way you travel in time. Try it for yourself on desktop or mobile!

Learning how to create an app in ChatGPT starts with the Jotform App Builder plugin (listed in ChatGPT's plugin directory as Jotform Apps): install it, connect a Jotform account, describe the app, approve the requested action, and refine the result. The plugin creates a Jotform App containing pages, forms, and resources that can be edited in Jotform App Builder and shared with its intended audience.

ChatGPT helps turn an idea into a clear request and supports revisions through conversation. The Jotform App Builder plugin performs the app-building actions, while the App Builder in Jotform provides the editor for closer customization.

This no-code ChatGPT app builder workflow suits projects built around information, forms, and everyday tasks.

"ChatGPT app development" can also describe coding projects. OpenAI's documentation on building plugins for ChatGPT describes a package of skills, an optional MCP server that connects to tools and data through the Model Context Protocol, optional UI, authentication, and publishing. The two routes differ like this:

This article covers the no-code route. The result is a Jotform App; the workflow does not include writing and deploying a separate codebase.

A Jotform App can organize pages, forms, and resources for customers, employees, members, or event attendees. The most useful first project has one audience and one clear purpose. Here are some examples:

These are starting structures. A booking form, for example, still needs its availability settings checked. An ordering app needs its order process reviewed, and any payment setup requires separate attention.

Setup starts with installing the plugin in ChatGPT and authorizing access to the intended Jotform account. Jotform's own how-to guide lists the steps.

To create an app in ChatGPT, select the installed plugin in a new chat and enter a specific description. Include the audience, purpose, pages, and design direction.

This gives the AI app builder a defined structure. The studio should then supply its real booking URL, approved resource links, contact details, and onboarding copy during review. It is important to review every generated form, link, and business rule before use.

A good prompt explains who will use the app, what they need to accomplish, and which elements support that task. Visual preferences help, but purpose and content should come first.

"Build an app for my business" leaves the audience, structure, and actions unclear. The design-studio example identifies a client audience, an onboarding task, specific pages, and a color scheme. Before submitting a request, define:

Request the essentials to build a Jotform App around one process, then expand.

The plugin supports follow-up requests in the same chat. Smaller changes make it easier to review each update and identify anything that needs correction. For the studio onboarding app, some follow-ups could include:

Each request should be followed by a review of the result. A map needs the correct address; a gallery needs suitable images; a booking form needs appropriate fields and configuration.

Select Edit in Jotform when you need closer editing. In Jotform App Builder, inspect every page, element, form, link, label, and visual choice. Replace the sample content and check that navigation follows the client's expected path. Third-party integrations require manual setup in the builder, so requesting a booking feature should not be treated as confirmation that an external calendar has been connected.

Select Share App in the generated result to open the available sharing options. For detailed distribution and access settings, open the app in Jotform App Builder and use the Publish tab and Quick Share. Jotform's sharing guide covers each option.

The builder supports copying the app link, inviting people by email, social sharing, and downloading a QR code. Choose the method that fits your audience: a client can receive a link, while event attendees may find a QR code more useful.

Review access before distributing the app, because newly created apps are public by default. Check exactly what a visitor can open before publishing.

Test the Jotform App as an intended user would, using fictional information first. Review it on both desktop and mobile before collecting real submissions.

Creating an app with the plugin is free to start, and Jotform offers a free Starter plan, but app usage remains subject to your account's allowances. A Jotform support reply from 2024 describes Starter as up to five forms and 100 monthly submissions. These are account allowances, rather than a separate allocation for each generated app, and they may have changed, so confirm them on Jotform's current pricing page. Paid plans provide more submissions.

Before you launch, compare expected usage with the current account limits. An onboarding app serving a few clients has different requirements from an event app collecting hundreds of registrations.

The most common mistakes are unclear requests, oversized first versions, and sharing before testing. Each can be reduced by defining a smaller task and reviewing the result.

This workflow is best for defined business tasks. Projects requiring extensive custom backend behavior need a separate assessment, such as the developer route described above.

Before sharing, confirm that the app serves its intended audience and that its content, behavior, and settings have been reviewed. A short launch checklist helps keep the review consistent.

#10449. Redmagic 12 Pro review: You’ve never gamed on a phone like this before

The Redmagic 12 Pro impresses with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, liquid cooling, a fan, plus a massive 8,400mAh battery to keep the games going for hours and hours.

As I sat in my living room with my family, playing Monster Hunter Outlanders together on the Redmagic 12 Pro, I completely forgot I was playing on a phone. The game looked perfect. It ran at a locked 60FPS and hadn’t dropped frames since I began playing over an hour ago. It just felt like I was back in college, playing Monster Hunter Freedom on my PSP with my friends in the same room.

Most other phones at this point would have throttled hard. What began at 60FPS almost certainly would have been 40FPS tops after 30 minutes or so; the frame drops during heavy fights would have been even worse, but the Redmagic 12 Pro didn’t skip a beat. Even after a solid hour of playing, the battery had only dropped 10%, completely erasing all concerns about using my phone as a gaming console.

This thing is the real deal, and while I’ve used plenty of high-performance phones and gaming phones over the years, none have quite nailed it as this one has. Now, with my Redmagic 12 Pro and my trusty GameSir G8 Galileo, I can game whenever and wherever I want without battery anxiety or thermal problems. Redmagic has gotten really good at this gaming thing.

Sustained gaming performance is difficult to pull off on a phone, which is why the Redmagic 12 Pro features two types of active cooling: a fan and liquid cooling. This design builds on last year’s with a larger liquid cooling system and a more efficient fan. The intake and exhaust vents are on the sides of the phone, not the back, ensuring these shouldn’t get easily blocked. Despite this, the phone is IP68 and IP69 rated.

Most modern phones have huge camera islands that make them awkward to use in controllers, but the Redmagic 12 Pro features a completely flat build that fits perfectly in *any* controller. I don’t usually like overly flat builds, but it actually suits this phone’s purpose.

This should mean the phone does exceedingly well in benchmarks, but I have the distinct feeling the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 processor inside is making that overly difficult. I don’t have any other SD8 Elite Gen 6 phones just yet, but rumor has it that this is one *hot* chipset. I saw the phone hit 50C during testing, so that definitely seems to be the case.

In 3DMark Solar Bay Extreme, a benchmark that stresses ray-tracing performance over 20 minutes, the Redmagic 12 Pro started at 2065 points and ended at 1169 on its last run. That’s a 43% drop in performance over a 20-minute period, which is in line with passively-cooled phones like the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Regardless, the initial performance is nearly double the S26 Ultra, while the 1169 end score matches the S26 Ultra’s best score and is roughly 35% higher than the S26 Ultra’s sustained performance score of around 860.

Actual gaming seemed to fare better in my testing, where I saw sustained performance consistently outperform any Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone I have in my possession. When running Wanderstop through the phone’s built-in Steam emulation (more on that soon), the Redmagic 12 Pro averaged 72FPS at the highest settings. Other phones with SD8 Elite Gen 5 processors scored half that, at best. Native Android games like Monster Hunter Outlanders worked even better.

But it’s not just performance that sets this phone apart; it’s the gaming features. Redmagic has fully leaned into the mobile gaming power user angle with its software. Pressing and holding the red button on the right side of the phone launches Gravity X, the built-in game launcher that keeps all your games in one place. It even features an embedded Steam emulator, so all you need to do is sign in with your Steam account and download anything in your library.

Overall performance on Steam games is impressive, but like any emulation, not everything is going to work. Hogwarts Legacy worked near-flawlessly at medium settings, but titles like Star Wars Galactic Racer wouldn’t run at all. Other apps that run Steam games, like DroidDeck and Game Native, also work, but the Adreno 850 GPU doesn’t have official support on those apps yet, so compatibility is very hit or miss (mostly miss) for now.

The Redmagic 12 Pro’s in-game menu is also unlike anything you’ve ever seen. It’s not just jam-packed with information, but has a boatload of bespoke features. One custom mapping tool lets you map the triggers (yes, this phone has capacitive triggers on the side) to any on-screen virtual key.

Another utility records all the time, Xbox/PS5/Switch style, and saves a clip at the touch of a floating button. Yet another features on on-screen AI anime character that can interact with your games and even give you gameplay feedback. You can even enable frame gen and Super Resolution in any game. It’s wild.

All this is wrapped up in an incredibly impressive hardware package, with loud, clear speakers, an excellent 185Hz AMOLED display (that uses DC dimming and 2160Hz PWM for eye comfort), with 5,000-nit peak brightness. I measured the actual HDR brightness at 2300-nits, so this can get nice and bright when it needs to.

If there was ever a phone that could play games and still get you through a full day’s normal phone usage, it’s this one. Passthrough charging is also supported, too, so you can keep the battery from getting overcharged or overheated while gaming for hours.

As is the case with many laser-focused devices like this, the camera is the low point of the experience. It’s got a 50MP rear camera and a 50MP ultra wide. Both get the job done, but they’ll never impress you.

The 16MP 9th-generation under display camera looks impressive on the surface — you can’t see it at all, even with light shining off the display — but the results are still far from good. Redmagic uses an AI algorithm to substantially enhance the overall quality, which cleans up the image nicely but exhibits lots of hallucinations. Just look at my eyes in the above picture. It’s not good.

Thankfully, the Android 17-based Redmagic OS 12 software is quite good. Visually, it reminds me of a mix of AOSP and Samsung’s One UI. Lots of expected features are here — an AI wallpaper generator, call screening, recording with transcripts, writing help, etc — plus all the awesome gaming-focused tools and quite a bit of customization across the OS.

It’s a great overall experience, but Redmagic only offers software updates for 3 years, so this one won’t stay around as long as some other phones. If you’re more interested in mobile gaming than anything — especially if you want a phone that can easily run Steam games in addition to mobile stuff — this is an impressively good choice.
